en: The Nī-karma (Bhikṣuṇī Karma), Volume One, with Preface, excerpted from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of the Western Taiyuan Monastery. Preface:
Originally, at the Deer Park and the Dragon City, the wondrous traces of the *śīla* (precepts) were initiated; at the Elephant Cave and Vulture Peak, [the path was opened...]
The profound essence of liberation:
thus, throughout the trichiliocosm, beings receive the refreshing coolness and emerge from the burning house;
from the heavens above and the earth below, they board the raft of precepts and cross the ford of delusion.
Consequently, the inner assembly flourished, and by this means, the outer disciples enjoyed peace and happiness.
Later, as the fine cotton of hidden truth was wrapped away, there arose the anxiety of the snapping axle of extensive learning;
as the subtle words of the Correct Teaching were concealed, the firmness of the life-preserving float was rarely seen.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa emerged preeminent, repairing the severed threads and seeking in emptiness;
Upāli’s work arose, shaking up the collapsed net and providing profound assistance.
Thus the torch of wisdom shone once more, and by this means the ocean of precepts was again purified.
The Vinaya teachings are vast and profound; it is truly difficult to enumerate them all exhaustively.

This *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure), however, is the orthodox method for perpetuating the tradition and the grand regulation for its protection. Its lineage traces back to the Five Sections (*pañcavargika*), and its source originates from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. It is indeed the essential pivot of Bodhi and the very ford for crossing over to Nirvana.

Having already applied my keen intellect since my youth to this profound purpose, I have contemplated the ultimate teachings and examined the paths of their meaning; though many years of shifting seasons have passed, I hope that I have not fallen into great error.

However, since ancient times, the various masters have differed in their interpretations; there are four primary versions of the *Karmavācanā* for the formal procedures (*saṃgha-karman*) of the Saṃgha.
Among these, those that are identical to the *Saṃgha-bhikṣu-vinaya* are not recorded separately;
those that differ are each categorized according to their type.

During the Sui dynasty, Vinaya Master Yuan standardized the *Karmavācanā* for the two divisions [of the Saṃgha], resulting in two separate volumes—one for monks and one for nuns—which were widely circulated. However, some later transmitters arbitrarily divided the rules for nuns into a third volume.
Furthermore, there was Guṇavarman of the Song dynasty, who compiled a single volume consisting of selected and distinct practices.
Su [Daoxuan] has thoroughly investigated all the various compilations; yet, in their collation of principles and search for textual accuracy, they contain many discrepancies and errors.

Thus, out of my own lack of talent, I have compiled a general account of the *bhikṣuṇī* discipline in three fascicles, binding them into a single work. I hope that by avoiding both addition and subtraction, it may suit the needs of the times; I have merely adopted established texts and do not dare to engage in forced interpretation.
I only pray that the pearl of the precepts may increase its radiance, shining in unison with the sun and moon;
and that the fragrant grass bound to my waist may transmit its excellence, decaying together with heaven and earth.
May those who view this in the future come to know this resolve.
1. Section on Expedient Means (Part One). Section on Expedient Means, First: Regarding the assembly of the Sangha, the Vinaya states:
"Those who ought to come, let them come."
It is further stated:
There are four kinds of Saṃghas—those consisting of four, five, ten, or twenty persons.

As for the Saṃgha of four persons, with the exception of the full ordination (*upasampadā*), the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*), and the absolution of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*), all other *karmans* should be performed.

Regarding a community of five monks: with the exception of receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*) and the formal act for absolution from offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*) in the Central Land, all other *karmavācanā* (formal monastic acts) should be performed.
Regarding a community of ten monks: with the exception of the formal act for absolution from offenses, all other *karmavācanā* should be performed.
Regarding a community of twenty monks: all *karmas* (formal acts) should be performed;
how much more so when there are more than twenty.
If, within any of the four categories of assemblies, there is even one person missing, the ritual procedure is not accomplished; it is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya.
Regarding "concordance" (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*):

the Vinaya states that it consists of performing a single *karmavācanā* while assembled in one place; those who have not arrived must have given their proxy consent (*anuśrāvaṇā*), and those present who ought to be censured are not censured.
It is further stated: Five things should be in concord:

if it is in accordance with the Dharma, one should be in concord; if one remains silent and acquiesces; if one has granted consent (*chanda*); if one has heard from a trustworthy person; or if one was previously sitting silently among them. These five matters should be in concord.
"Those who have not yet received the full precepts must leave.
The Vinaya states:
"One should not perform a *karmavācanā* or recite the *Poṣadha* in the presence of those who have not received the full precepts."
It is further stated:
"Listen; except for those who have not yet received the full ordination (*upasampadā*), the rest shall perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts in their presence.
It is also stated:
There are four cases regarding the fulfillment of the quorum:

there is one who has attained the quorum and should not be censured; there is one who has not attained the quorum and should be censured; there is one who has not attained the quorum and should not be censured; and there is one who has attained the quorum and should be censured.
What kind of person, having completed the required number [of witnesses], should not be censured?

One for whom a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), or *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople) has been performed.
What kind of person, though not completing the quorum, should be censured?
It is one who wishes to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
What kind of person neither completes the quorum nor should be censured?

If a *karmavācanā* (formal act) is being performed for a *bhikṣuṇī*, a *bhikṣu* may not count toward the quorum, nor may he object. This applies to: a *śikṣamāṇā*; a *śrāmaṇera*; a *śrāmaṇerī*; the thirteen types of persons such as one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; one who has been suspended (*ukkhepaniya*); one who has been expelled (*nihsrāvaṇīya*); one who is subject to expulsion; one who is living apart (*parivāsa*); one who is on the boundary of the *sīmā*; one who is in the air by means of psychic power (*ṛddhi*); one who has become invisible; one who is beyond the range of sight or hearing; or the very person for whom the *karmavācanā* is being performed.
What kind of person fulfills the required number and yet may be censured?

It is a virtuous bhikṣuṇī who resides within the same boundary, who does not use supernormal powers to remain in the air, who does not conceal herself, and who does not move beyond the range of sight or hearing, even to the point of speaking to a bystander.
Have the bhikṣuṇīs who have not arrived declared their *chanda* (consent) and *viśuddhi* (purity)?
With the sole exception of those within a defined boundary (*sīmā*), they may not declare their *chanda*;
their *chanda* must be declared together with their *viśuddhi*.
When it is time for the *pravāraṇā*, one should say, "I grant my consent for the *pravāraṇā*.
If there are matters concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha; matters of illness; or circumstances involving the care of the sick, it is permitted to grant consent.
The Vinaya states:
There are five ways of giving one's consent (*chanda*):

saying "I give my consent to you," saying "I speak my consent," saying "I speak my consent for your sake," manifesting the physical signs of giving consent, or speaking at length about giving consent.

If one does not manifest their physical form or verbally express their consent (*chanda*), the giving of consent is not accomplished. One should instead give consent to another. If the person holding the consent dies after receiving it; or if they go elsewhere; or if they abandon the path (*pravrajyā*);

or if they enter the assembly of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); or if they enter the assembly of a separate faction (*nikāya*); or if they arrive at the boundary of the *sīmā*; or if dawn breaks; or if they themselves declare that they have committed one of the thirteen grave offenses (*antimāpatti*); or if they have been suspended (*utkṣipta*); or if they have been expelled (*pravrājita*); or if they are subject to expulsion; or if they are in the air by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*); or if they are out of sight and hearing—the giving of consent is not accomplished, and one should instead give consent to another.
If one reaches the midst of the community or the midst of the Saṃgha, it is also like this.
If one wishes to communicate a formal proposal (*chanda*) in detail, one should go to the person who is to transmit the proposal and, having performed the proper ritual gestures, speak as follows:
"Sister, please attend to me with a single mind!"
"I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], regarding a matter of the Saṃgha that accords with the Dharma, grant my consent and purity.
At that time, if the bhikṣuṇī holding the consent has her own business arise and is unable to go to the Saṃgha, she is permitted to transfer the consent to another person.
When transferring it, one should say:
"Sister, please attend to me with single-mindedness!
I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], am conveying the consent and purity of Bhikṣuṇī [Name]."
Both she and I, regarding the affairs of the Dharma and the Saṃgha, grant our consent and purity.
When the bhikṣuṇī holding the consent arrives at the Saṃgha and speaks, if she is able to remember their names, she shall address the Saṃgha one by one, calling out their names and saying:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!"
The bhikṣuṇī so-and-so and the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so grant their consent and purity for the legal business of the Saṃgha.
If one cannot record their names, simply say "many."

If a person who has received the consent (*chandadāna*) falls asleep, enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), forgets, or does not intentionally act in such a way, it is considered that the consent has been granted;
however, if they intentionally fail to communicate it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"What is the Sangha currently doing?
There are three kinds of activities:
first, those concerning human affairs, such as receiving a confession."
Second, matters concerning insentient things, such as the tying together of various boundaries.
Third, matters concerning both sentient and insentient things, such as the distribution of dwellings or the separation from one's robes.
Since these matters to be performed must be deliberated upon by the Saṃgha to determine what is appropriate, it is necessary to question those involved regarding their actions before the assembly.
Regarding *karmavācanā*:
in terms of their essential nature, there are only three types, namely:
the single motion (*jñapti*), the motion followed by one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya*), and the motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha*).
The Vinaya states: There are seven kinds of *karmas* that should not be performed: a *karman* that is neither according to the Dharma nor the Vinaya;

a *karman* that is neither according to the Dharma and is performed by a separate assembly; a *karman* that is neither according to the Dharma and is performed by a harmonious assembly; a *karman* that is according to the Dharma and is performed by a separate assembly; a *karman* that is similar to being according to the Dharma and is performed by a separate assembly; a *karman* that is similar to being according to the Dharma and is performed by a harmonious assembly; and a *karman* of censure that is not brought to cessation.
One should perform the formal act (karmavācanā) in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya:
for a motion-and-one-vote (jñapti-dvitīya-karman), one should make the motion according to the rules for making a motion and perform the formal act according to the rules for performing a formal act;
the same applies to a motion-and-three-votes (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
This constitutes a formal act (kamma) that is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
These six expedients apply universally to all other legal matters, with the sole exception of the delimitation of boundaries; if any are missing, the act is not validly accomplished.
2. Chapter on Establishing Boundaries (Part One). Chapter Two: Establishing the Great Boundary (*Mahā-sīmā*). The Vinaya states:
One should spread out seats, strike the *gandī* gong, and assemble together in one place; the acceptance of proxy consent (*chanda*) is not permitted.

Among these, the resident bhikṣuṇīs should proclaim the characteristics of the four sides of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*): if there is a mountain in the east, they should call it a mountain; if there is a moat, they should call it a moat; likewise for a city, a field boundary, a garden, a grove, a pond, a tree, a rock, a wall, or a shrine.
As with the characteristics in the east, so it is for the other directions.

However, at the place where boundaries are demarcated, two boundaries must not touch one another; a space should be left between them. Furthermore, one must not demarcate a boundary across a swift-flowing stream, except where there is a permanent bridge or boat service.
Regarding the method for proclaiming the boundaries: one should rise and pay homage to the Saṃgha, and declare:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!

I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], who is a resident (if not a resident, one who knows the boundaries should proclaim them), shall proclaim the characteristics of the four sides of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) for the Saṃgha. [If not a resident, the two words "resident" (*jù zhù*) should be omitted.]
Having made the announcement, one should chant [the formal motion], chanting in order starting from the southeast corner and so forth, until it has been recited three times.

From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā*—whether he be a senior elder (*sthavira*), a junior elder, one who recites the Vinaya, or one who does not—should act in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This resident bhikṣuṇī has proclaimed the marks of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) in the four directions.

If the time is right for the Sangha, and if the Sangha is willing to grant its consent, let the Sangha now establish a great boundary within these marks of the four directions, constituting a single residence and a single recitation of the precepts.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
This resident bhikṣuṇī is proclaiming the boundary markers for the great perimeter (mahā-sīmā) in the four directions."
The Saṃgha now establishes a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) within these four markers, constituting a single residence and a single recitation of the precepts.

Any of you, sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha’s establishment of a great boundary within these four markers as a single residence and a single recitation of the precepts, remain silent; any who do not consent, speak.

The Sangha has already consented to this: within these four boundaries, they shall dwell in a single residence and perform the Uposatha together. The formal establishment of the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) is now complete.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the method for dissolving the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*): if various bhikṣuṇīs wish to enlarge or narrow the boundary, the Buddha permits that they first dissolve the previous boundary; thereafter, they may enlarge or narrow it according to their intention.
It should be resolved by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*; it should be performed in this manner:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!
Now, in this residence, the bhikṣuṇīs dwell together and perform the *poṣadha* recitation together."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, the boundary shall be dissolved.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣuṇīs residing in this dwelling place, who share the same residence and the same recitation of the precepts, now dissolve the boundary (*sīmā*).
Those of you, sisters, who consent for the Saṃgha to dissolve the boundary of those sharing the same residence and the same recitation of the precepts, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already granted its consent to dissolve the boundary for those dwelling in the same residence and reciting the Prātimokṣa together.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held as such.

The Method for Establishing a Boundary for a Unified Uposatha and a Unified Distribution of Offerings: If two residences have separate distributions of offerings and separate Uposathas, and the bhikṣuṇīs wish to establish a common boundary for a unified Uposatha and a unified distribution of offerings, [the following procedure shall be followed].
The Buddha permitted that each should first dissolve their own boundary, and then perform the formal act of proclamation and resolution (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to establish it.
The arrangement of seats and other preparations should be as previously described;
it should be performed in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

As has been described regarding the characteristics of the boundary, if the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha grants its consent, let the Sangha now establish, at this place and that place, a single boundary for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa and a single boundary for the sharing of material offerings.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

According to the characteristics of the boundary as described, the Sangha now establishes at this place and that place a single boundary for the recitation of the precepts and a single boundary for the sharing of offerings."

"Venerable sisters, those who consent to the Saṃgha's formal delimitation of a boundary such that there shall be a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa and a single distribution of offerings at this place and that place, please remain silent; those who do not consent, please speak."
The Sangha has already consented that in this place and that place, there shall be a single recitation of the *Poṣadha* and a single distribution of offerings, and the boundary has been established.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The Method for Establishing a Single Boundaries for the Uposatha and Separate Boundaries for Alms: If two residences have separate Uposathas and separate boundaries for alms, and one wishes to establish a single boundary for the Uposatha while maintaining separate boundaries for alms, [one should proceed as follows].
First, each person shall dissolve their own boundary, and then the new one shall be established.
The method of establishment is the same as before, with only this single phrase being changed:
"One *poṣadha* recitation, separate offerings."
The declaration is as follows:

The legal procedure for establishing a boundary where the *poṣadha* is recited separately but the *lābha* (alms-offerings) are shared in common. If two residences have separate *poṣadha* recitations and separate *lābha*, and the bhikṣuṇīs desire to have a separate *poṣadha* while sharing the same *lābha*—for the purpose of protecting their residence—[the following should be performed].
The Buddha has permitted the formal act of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) for such a binding; it should be performed as follows:
"Listen, sisters of the Saṃgha!

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now, at this and that dwelling place, establish a separate recitation of the Prātimokṣa while sharing a common distribution of offerings (*lābha*), for the purpose of protecting and maintaining the dwellings."
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

Now, for the sake of protecting this and that residence, the Saṃgha shall establish separate recitations of the Prātimokṣa at these respective dwellings, while sharing the same distribution of offerings."

Whichever sisters approve of the Saṃgha’s formal resolution to hold separate recitations of the Prātimokṣa at these two residences while sharing the same communal offerings for the sake of protecting the dwellings, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let her speak.

The Saṃgha has already consented; at this and that residence, the separate recitation of the Prātimokṣa has been concluded with a common distribution of offerings for the sake of guarding the residence.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding this and the two preceding cases, the Vinaya contains no method for their dissolution. If one wishes to dissolve them, the dissolution should be performed by reversing the procedure used for their formal establishment (*sīmā-bandha*); the reversal should be understood accordingly.

As for the method of establishing a *karmavastu* boundary (*śīmaṇḍala*), if there are four, five, ten, or twenty persons present when a *karma* (formal act) arises, the large assembly gathered therein will become utterly exhausted.

The Buddha permitted the establishment of a *sīmā* (boundary) by designating the characteristics of a small boundary for the four directions, using such markers as stakes, stones, or field boundaries to establish the limits.
Within this area, one should establish three layers of boundary markers:
the innermost layer constitutes the characteristics of the *śīla-sīmā* (precept boundary).
The middle layer represents the internal boundary of the *mahā-sīmā*; this must not overlap with or run parallel to the boundary of the *sīmā-maṇḍala*, and a space should be left between them.
The outermost layer represents the external boundary of the *mahā-sīmā*.
First, announce the boundaries of the *sīmā* (precept-field) and perform the formal act as prescribed above.
It should be done in this manner:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!..."
The bhikṣuṇīs of this residence have declared the boundaries of the small four-sided area.
If the Saṃgha is ready and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now establish a *karmavācanā* site (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) within these declared boundaries of the small four-sided area.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This resident bhikṣuṇī has proclaimed the marks of the small boundary for the four directions."
The Saṃgha now intends to establish a *sīmā* (boundary for the observance of the precepts) within these four marks of the small boundary.
Those of you, venerable sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha establishing a *sīmā* within these four marks, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already consented to demarcate the boundary for the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (precept-field) within these four directional markers;
since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Next, the internal and external markers of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) are announced and demarcated as previously described.

The text for the procedure of dissolving the *śīmaṇḍala* (boundary) is abbreviated and does not include the dissolution formula. If one wishes to dissolve it, one should reverse the formula for its establishment as follows:
"Listen, sisters of the Saṃgha!
This is the *śīmaṇḍala* for the bhikṣuṇīs at this residence."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the *sīmā* (boundary) be dissolved.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!..."
This is the *śīma* (boundary) for the *bhikṣuṇīs* at this residence; the Saṃgha now dissolves this *śīma*.
Whoever among the sisters approves of the Saṃgha dissolving the *śīma* here, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented; the lifting of the *kṣetrasīmā* (boundary of the training ground) is now concluded.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the method for establishing a small boundary (*sīman*) to confer the precepts: if there is one who wishes to receive the precepts and goes outside the boundary, and a bhikṣuṇī goes there to obstruct them.
The Buddha said:
"If there are those who do not agree and have not yet left the boundary, they are permitted to quickly assemble in one place outside the boundary and establish a small boundary (kṣudrasīmā).
It should be done in this manner."
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
The Sangha has gathered in one place to establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*).
If it is the time for the Sangha and the Sangha consents, let the Sangha authorize the establishment of this small boundary.
The motion is thus stated.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
Now this Sangha assembles in one place to establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*).
"Whichever sisters approve of the Saṃgha's assembly in one place to bind a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak.
The Saṃgha has approved and completed the binding of the small boundary."
Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the method for resolving a difficult situation by dissolving a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) to confer the precepts: one should not depart without first dissolving the boundary.
It should be understood in this way:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
Now the assembly of monks has gathered to dissolve the boundary."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to dissolve the boundary.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
Now the community of monks has assembled to dissolve the boundary.
Which of you sisters who consent to the community dissolving the boundary remain silent; which do not consent, speak up.
The community has consented and the dissolution of the boundary is complete.
The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is upheld as such.
Regarding the legal procedure for establishing a small boundary (*kṣudrakasīman*) to recite the Prātimokṣa:

the Vinaya rules state that on the day of the Uposatha, when traveling through a wilderness area where there is no village, the community of monks (*saṃgha*) should assemble together in one place to recite the precepts collectively.

If the Saṃgha cannot achieve harmony, those who follow the same Upādhyāya and others should immediately proceed to gather in one place and establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) to recite the Prātimokṣa.
It should be established in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
Now there are this many bhikṣuṇīs assembled.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant permission, let us establish a small boundary (sīmā).
The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
Now there are this many bhikṣuṇīs gathered to establish a small boundary (sīmā)."
"Whichever sisters approve of this assembly of so many bhikṣuṇīs binding a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) remain silent; whoever does not approve should speak.
The Sangha has approved, and this assembly of so many bhikṣuṇīs has finished binding the small boundary."
Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the method for resolving difficulties by dissolving a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) to recite the *Prātimokṣa*: one must not depart without first dissolving the boundary.
It should be understood in this way:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
Now there are this many bhikṣuṇīs assembled."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha hear me: I announce that this small boundary (sīmā) at this place is hereby dissolved.
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
Now that this many bhikṣuṇīs have assembled, the small boundary (sīmā) of this place shall be dissolved.
Which of you, venerable sisters, approves of the Sangha dissolving the small boundary of this place? Those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve speak.
The Sangha has already consented to the resolution of this small boundary (sīmā) here.
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the method for establishing a small boundary for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) in difficult circumstances: if there are many bhikṣuṇīs traveling on a road in a non-village area where no boundary has been established on the day of the *pravāraṇā*.
If they can perform the *pravāraṇā* in harmony, it is well;

if they cannot achieve harmony, then according to those who share the same *upādhyāya* and so forth, they should move to another location, establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), and perform the *pravāraṇā*.
It should be done in this manner:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
The seating places for the bhikṣuṇīs are already full, extending as far as these seating places of the bhikṣuṇīs."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha now establish a small boundary (sīmā) at this location.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
"Marking the boundary at this place where these bhikṣuṇīs are seated, the Saṃgha shall establish a small boundary (sīmā) here.
Sisters who consent to marking the boundary at this place where these bhikṣuṇīs are seated, so that the Saṃgha may establish a small boundary here, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak."
The Saṃgha has consented; the small boundary (sīmā) has been established for the seating area of these bhikṣuṇīs.
Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter shall be held thus.
The Method for Resolving Difficulties by Establishing a Small Boundary for the *Pravāraṇā*: One should not depart without first relinquishing the boundary.
It should be relinquished in this manner:
"Listen, noble sisters of the Saṃgha!"
The seating area for these bhikṣuṇīs is thus defined.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now dissolve this small boundary (kṣudraka-sīmā).
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
Within these sitting places of the bhikṣuṇīs, the Sangha now dissolves this minor boundary (sīmā).
Venerable Sisters who consent to the Sangha dissolving the minor boundary within these sitting places of the bhikṣuṇīs remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has consented; the boundary for the seating area of these bhikṣuṇīs has been dissolved.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The Procedure for Establishing the Boundaries of the "Non-separation from Robes" (Akaṭhinīya-sīmā): If there is a bhikṣuṇī who desires solitude and thinks to herself, "I must not sleep apart from my robes," she may request that the boundaries of the non-separation from robes be established through a formal motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
It should be done in this manner:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This location constitutes a single residential area for the purpose of reciting the Prātimokṣa together."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of its forbearance, grant permission to establish the *acīvarāpatti-sīmā*.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
In this place, which is a single residence and a single assembly for the recitation of the precepts, the Saṃgha now establishes a boundary for not losing one's robe.

Those of you, sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha’s establishment of a boundary for not losing one's robe in this place—a single residence and a single assembly for the recitation of the precepts—remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented; at this place, within the same residence and for the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa, the boundary for not losing one's robes has been established.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
If there is a village within the boundary, one should perform the formal act of demarcating the area excluding the village and its surroundings.
The procedure for the formal act is as described above, with the addition of one sentence stating:
"excluding the village and the area surrounding the village."
The motion is as follows.

Regarding the ritual for dissolving the *acīvarāpattika-sīmā* (the boundary where one is not subject to the offense of being without robes), the text is abbreviated and omits the dissolution; it should be translated from the formula for establishing [the boundary] as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!..."
In this place, which constitutes a single residence and a single recitation of the precepts,
if the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the boundary of "not losing one's robe" be dissolved.
The motion is as follows.
Venerable Sisters, listen!
At this location, which constitutes a single residence and a single recitation of the precepts, the Saṃgha now dissolves the *acīvaramuṭṭhāna-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robe).

Venerable Sisters who consent to the Saṃgha’s dissolution of the *acīvaramuṭṭhāna-sīmā* at this location—a single residence with a single recitation of the precepts—remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented that this place shall be a single residence with a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa, and the boundary for not losing one's robes has been dissolved.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
There is a method for resolving [conflicts] in a village, the reverse of which is also the same as this.

Regarding the method for demarcating a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*): if there is no place for preparing food within a monastery, the Buddha permitted that a formal motion and second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) be made to demarcate a pure area. One should announce the name of the room, or the storehouse, or the heated hall, or the walking path (*caṅkrama*).

Once a bhikṣuṇī has risen, she should perform the proper rites within the saṃgha and announce that the courtyard and the locations for various fruits, vegetables, and so forth are to be designated as pure ground (śuddhasthāna).
Having made the announcement, it should be performed in this manner.
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now demarcate a certain place as pure ground (śuddhasthāna).
This is the formal motion (jñapti)."
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
The Sangha now demarcates a certain area to establish it as a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*).
Those venerable sisters who consent to the Sangha’s demarcation of this area as a pure ground should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to demarcate such-and-such a place as a purified area (śuddhasthāna).
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The Vinaya states:
There are four kinds of pure grounds (*śuddhasthāna*).
First, when a donor or a supervisor is constructing a monastery (*saṃghārāma*), they designate it by saying:
"This place is to be made a pure ground for the Saṃgha."
Second, if one has built a monastery for the Saṃgha but has not yet bestowed it upon the Saṃgha;
third, if it has half a fence, or mostly no fence, or none at all; and the same applies to walls or moats.
Fourth, regarding the method for the Saṃgha to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to demarcate a pure area (*śuddha-sthāna*):
the text omits the procedure for its dissolution. One should reverse the formula for its demarcation as follows:
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!..."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now release the pure ground at such-and-such a place.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now releases the pure ground at such-and-such a place.
Those of you, Venerable Sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha’s release of the pure ground at such-and-such a place, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has completed its consent to release the pure ground at such-and-such a place.
The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is upheld as such. 3.
Chapter on Bestowing the Precepts (Part One). Chapter Three: The Eight Rules Regarding the Bestowal of Precepts that Must Not Be Transgressed. According to the Vinaya:
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred Śākya women, went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and said:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will grant permission for women to leave the household life and enter the path within the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha said:
“Stop, Gotamī! Do not speak such words, desiring that women be allowed to go forth and practice the Path.”
For what reason? Gautamī!
If women were to go forth from home into the path within the Buddha-dharma, it would cause the Buddha-dharma not to endure for long.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Mahāprajāpatī prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.

Later, on another occasion, Mahāprajāpatī again went with five hundred Śākya women; they had all shaved their heads and donned the saṃghāṭī robes. They proceeded to the Jeta Grove Monastery and stood outside the gate, their feet blistered from walking and their bodies covered in dust, weeping and shedding tears.
At that time, Ānanda, having seen this, went to inquire and requested [instruction] from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One expounded for him the eight dharmas that must not be transgressed; if one is able to practice them, that is itself the going forth and the receiving of the precepts.
Therefore, it was said: "Ānanda!
I now establish for women eight rules to be observed for as long as life lasts, which must not be transgressed; if one can practice them, that constitutes receiving the precepts."
What are the eight?

Although she may be a bhikṣuṇī of a hundred years' standing, upon seeing a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts, she should rise to meet him, pay homage, and provide a clean seat for him to sit upon;
such a rule should be respected, honored, and praised, and must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
A bhikṣuṇī should not revile or scold a bhikṣu, nor should she slander him by saying:
"He has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his dignified conduct.
These rules should be respected as above.

A bhikṣuṇī should not perform an *uddhava* (formal charge) against a bhikṣu, nor remind him of an offense, nor make a formal admission on his behalf; she should not obstruct another’s search for an offense, nor obstruct the *poṣadha*, nor obstruct the *pravāraṇā*. A bhikṣuṇī should not reprove a bhikṣu; rather, it is the bhikṣu who should reprove the bhikṣuṇī.
This rule should be respected as previously described.
Once a śikṣamāṇā has completed her training in the precepts, she shall request the higher ordination from the community of bhikṣus;
this rule regarding respect and so forth is as described above.
When a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must perform the mānatva penance before both communities of monks and nuns.
This rule should be respected, etc., as stated above.
A bhikṣuṇī should request instruction from the Saṃgha every half-month;
this rule should be respected, etc., as stated above.
A bhikṣuṇī should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where there are no bhikṣus;
this rule should be respected as above.
When the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha has completed the summer retreat, they should request the three matters for self-examination (pravāraṇā) from within the bhikṣu saṃgha.
"Seeing, hearing, and doubting;
such dharmas should be respected, etc., as stated above.

Thus, Ānanda, I now declare these eight dharmas that must not be transgressed. If a woman is able to practice them, it constitutes the reception of the precepts—just as a person builds a bridge over a great body of water and crosses it."
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
I have now declared these eight rules that must not be transgressed for women; if they can practice them, this constitutes the reception of the precepts.
At that time, having heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, Ānanda went to Mahāprajāpatī and said to her:

“Women may go forth from home into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma and receive the full precepts; the World-Honored One has established for women eight rules that must not be transgressed, and if they can practice these, it constitutes the reception of the precepts.”
He then explained those eight matters to her as above. Mahāprajāpatī said:
"If the World-Honored One has taught these eight rules that must not be transgressed for women, I and the five hundred Śākya women shall together receive them upon our heads."
Ānanda returned once more and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: “It is so, Ānanda!”
Mahāprajāpatī and five hundred women have received the precepts.
He further told Ānanda:
“If women had not gone forth in the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha-dharma would have remained for five hundred years longer.”
Upon hearing this, Ānanda was displeased; harboring regret and distress in his heart, he wept with streaming tears, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.
Regarding the procedure for bestowing the precepts upon those who have come well, according to the Vinaya:

at that time, the listeners of the Dharma, while still seated, were cleansed of all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, accomplished the various dharmas, and already obtained the fruit, they came forward and said to the Buddha:
"We now wish to go forth under the Tathāgata to practice the holy life."
The Buddha said: "Come, bhikṣuṇī!
In my Dharma, enjoy yourself fully; practice the holy life and bring an end to the source of suffering."

Having uttered these words, his hair fell away naturally, the *kāṣāya* robe was donned upon his body, and an alms bowl appeared in his hand; this is what is called "leaving the household life" and receiving the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*).

Regarding the legal rules for conferring the precepts through the ritual of *karmavācanā* and ordaining others, the World-Honored One established the precepts: "Although I have permitted you to ordain others, you are foolish and recklessly ordain people without knowing how to instruct them."

Because they do not understand the instructions, they do not maintain dignified deportment; they beg for alms improperly, accepting impure food from various places or receiving food in an impure bowl; and during the morning and midday meals, they shout and clamor loudly, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly.
From this day forward, it is permitted for the Saṃgha to confer full ordination through a formal motion with one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
Having gone into that Saṃgha, one should perform the ritual with proper decorum and make this request:
"May the noble Saṃgha listen!..."

I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], request the Saṃgha to grant me permission to ordain others by bestowing the full precepts. May the Saṃgha listen to me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], as I ordain others by bestowing the full precepts.

After this has been said three times, the Saṃgha should examine this person. If she is incapable of being instructed, and cannot be provided with the two-year training in the precepts and the two methods of inclusion, one should say to her: "Sister!..."
"Stop; do not ordain others.
If one possesses the wisdom and capability to instruct, and has two years of training in the precepts as well as the two methods of integration, one should act in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī [Name], now requests from the Saṃgha the authorization to confer full ordination upon others.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now authorize this bhikṣuṇī [Name] to confer full ordination upon others.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
This bhikṣuṇī [Name], now requests from the Saṃgha the authorization to bestow full ordination upon another."
The Saṃgha now intends to grant full ordination to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so for the sake of others.
Those of you, venerable sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha granting full ordination to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so for the sake of others, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has already granted its assent that the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has finished bestowing full ordination upon another person.
Since the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The same rule applies to the *upādhyāyī* (preceptor).
Regarding the ordination of śrāmaṇerikās and the rules concerning those who resemble them in form, the Vinaya states:
"If one wishes to have one's hair shaved within the bhikṣuṇī monastery, one should inform the Saṃgha, or speak to each individual to let them know."
One should announce to the Saṃgha as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!
This person, so-and-so, wishes to seek a haircut from so-and-so."
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent that the hair of so-and-so be shaved.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, one should then shave the hair.

Regarding the procedure for ordaining a śrāmaṇerī and requesting a precept-mother (upādhyāyinī) according to the Dharma: if one intends to receive ordination within a bhikṣuṇī monastery, one must first request a precept-mother.
Performing the ritual with proper decorum, one should make this request:
"Sister, attend to me with a single mind!
I, [Name], now seek you, Venerable Sister, to be my Preceptor for the Ten Precepts; may you, Venerable Sister, act as my Preceptor for the Ten Precepts."
"Because of you, Ayyā, I have been able to receive the śrāmaṇerī precepts; out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.
She should reply:
It may be so. Please perform the formal request according to the ritual: "Sister, please attend to me with a single mind!
I, [Name], now seek you, Venerable Sister, to be my Preceptor for the Ten Precepts; I pray that you will act as my Preceptor for the Ten Precepts."
"Because of you, Ayyā, I have been able to receive the śrāmaṇerī precepts; out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.
She should reply:
It may be so. Regarding the procedure for announcing to the Saṃgha: if harmony cannot be achieved, one should inform the entire Saṃgha;
if harmony is achieved, one should make the following announcement:
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to go forth from the household life under the guidance of so-and-so.
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to grant permission, let the Sangha allow so-and-so to go forth.
The declaration is thus.
Regarding the procedure for bestowing the precepts: have them don the *kāṣāya* and, assuming the proper deportment, speak as follows:
"I, the venerable nun [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha."
I now follow the Buddha to leave the household life; [my] precept-nurse is [named] So-and-so. The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One.
(Recite this three times.)
I, [Name], my aunt, have completed taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Having now followed the Buddha into homelessness, I take [Name], the Bhikṣuṇī, as my preceptor; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One.
Recite this three times.
Then, speak the words for conferring the ten precepts:
"For as long as life lasts, do not kill living beings."
"Can you uphold these śrāmaṇerī precepts?
She replies, "I can."
"For as long as life lasts, you must not steal.
This is a precept for a śrāmaṇerikā; can you uphold it?
She replies:
"Yes. For as long as life lasts, one must not engage in sexual misconduct.
This is a śrāmaṇerikā precept; can you uphold it?"
He replied: "I can.
For as long as life lasts, I shall not speak falsely."
"Can you uphold these śrāmaṇerī precepts?
She replies, "I can."
"For as long as life lasts, one must not drink alcohol.
This is a precept for a śrāmaṇerikā; can you uphold it?
She replied:
Yes. For as long as life lasts, you must not wear flower garlands or apply fragrant oils to your body.
This is a śrāmaṇerikā precept; can you uphold it?
He replied: "I can.
For as long as life lasts, I shall not engage in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor shall I go to witness or listen to them."
"Are you able to uphold these śrāmaṇerī precepts?
She replies,
"I am able."
"For as long as life lasts, one must not sit upon high, wide, or large beds.
This is a śrāmaṇerikā precept; can you uphold it?
She replies:
Yes. For as long as life lasts, one must not eat at improper times.
This is a precept for a śrāmaṇerikā; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can.
For as long as life lasts, I shall not grasp or hold gold, silver, or precious objects, whether in their raw or wrought state."
"Are you able to uphold these śrāmaṇerī precepts?
She replies,
"I am able."
These are the ten precepts for a śrāmaṇerī.
For as long as life lasts, you must not transgress them; can you uphold them?
She replies:
Yes. You have now completed receiving the precepts; you should make offerings to the Triple Gem and diligently cultivate the three types of action:
practicing seated meditation, reciting the sutras, and assiduously performing communal duties.
Having bestowed [the precepts], he instructed him to recite ten items.

These ten are: first, all sentient beings depend upon food and drink; second, name-and-form; third, the three feelings; fourth, the four noble truths; fifth, the five aggregates; sixth, the six sense bases; seventh, the seven factors of enlightenment; eighth, the eightfold noble path; ninth, the nine abodes of sentient beings; tenth, the ten totalities.

Regarding the procedure for converting non-Buddhists: if there is a non-Buddhist who wishes to seek ordination, the Sangha shall grant them a four-month period of probation through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation).
It should be granted as follows:
after first shaving their hair and donning the *kāṣāya*, up until they join their palms, they are instructed to speak these words:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
I, [Name], formerly of the non-Buddhist path, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha.
I seek from the World-Honored One to go forth into homelessness for the sake of the Way; the World-Honored One is my Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Recite this three times:
"I, [Name], a follower of external paths, have taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
I go forth from home to study the Path under the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is my truly real, perfectly awakened one."
Recite this three times.
Next, confer the characteristics of the precepts; the ritual for conferring them is the same as above.
Following the ritual for the four-month co-residence, one should next instruct [the candidate] to speak these words:
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
I, the outsider named [Name], request from the Saṃgha four months of co-residence.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me four months of co-residence.
Recite this three times.
Having placed [the object] in a place where it is visible to the eyes but not audible to the ears, the Saṃgha should perform the following rite:
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!..."
That certain outsider now requests from the community of monks a four-month period of co-residence.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant permission, let the Saṃgha grant that certain outsider a four-month period of co-residence.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
That certain outsider now requests from the community of monks a four-month period of co-residence."
The Saṃgha now grants him a four-month period of co-residence.
Those of you, Venerable Sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha granting him a four-month period of co-residence, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already granted that outsider the four-month period of probation;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent. This matter is thus upheld.
Once he has completed his probation and has caused the bhikṣuṇīs to be joyful in heart, he shall then receive full ordination within the Sangha.
Why is it that these non-Buddhists cannot cause the bhikṣuṇīs’ minds to rejoice?

Because those non-Buddhists, by their very nature, stubbornly cling to the ways of non-Buddhist laypeople; they do not associate with the bhikṣuṇīs but associate with non-Buddhists, they do not comply with the bhikṣuṇīs, and they recite and study heterodox doctrines.
If they hear someone speak ill of the non-Buddhists, they immediately give rise to anger; if they hear someone disparage the teachings of the non-Buddhist masters, they likewise give rise to anger.

If heterodox practitioners come and praise the excellent qualities of their own path, they rejoice and leap for joy; if a teacher of a heterodox school comes and hears praise for the matters of his own path, he likewise rejoices and leaps for joy;
even if he hears it said that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are not the true Dharma, he still rejoices and leaps for joy.
This is what is meant by saying that such heterodox practitioners cannot cause the bhikṣuṇīs to find true delight.
How is it that the non-Buddhists can cause the bhikṣuṇīs to rejoice?
It is the reverse of the above.
This is called dwelling together with the non-Buddhists, harmonizing their minds and intentions, and causing the bhikṣuṇīs to rejoice.
Regarding the legal rules for the two-year training in the precepts:

it is permitted for a girl who is eighteen years old to undergo two years of training in the precepts; once she has completed them and reached twenty years of age, she shall be granted the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

If she is ten years old and has previously been married, she is permitted to undergo two years of training in the precepts; once she has completed them and reached twelve years of age, she may receive the full ordination.
The two-year training in the precepts should be granted in this manner:
the śrāmaṇerikā should go before the Saṃgha and, having performed the formal ritual, address them, saying:
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, the śrāmaṇerikā [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, with the bhikṣuṇī [Name] as my upādhyāyikā.
May the Saṃgha grant me the two-year training in the precepts out of compassion.
This is said three times.
Having led the śrāmaṇerikā away to a place where she cannot hear but can see, the one who presides over the legal procedure within the assembly should act as follows:
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This śrāmaṇerikā so-and-so now requests from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, with the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as her preceptor (upādhyāyikā).
If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant this śrāmaṇerikā so-and-so the two-year training in the precepts, with the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as her preceptor.
The motion is thus:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
This śrāmaṇerikā so-and-so now requests from the Sangha the two-year training in the precepts, with the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as her preceptor."
The Saṃgha now grants two years of training in the precepts to this śrāmaṇerikā [Name], with [Name] as her precept-mother (upādhyāyinī).

Those of you, venerable sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha granting two years of training in the precepts to this śrāmaṇerikā [Name] with [Name] as her precept-mother, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
This has been stated three times.
The Saṃgha has granted the two-year training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerikā [Name], with [Name] as her preceptress (upādhyāyinī).
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
He imparts the discourse corresponding to the six dharmas, saying:
"Listen attentively, [Name]!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught six dharmas."
One must not commit impure conduct or engage in sexual intercourse.
If a śikṣamāṇā engages in sexual intercourse,
she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā and is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
If one touches the body of a man with a defiled mind, one commits a transgression of the precepts and should receive the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit such an offense; can you uphold this?
He replied: "I can.
I shall not commit theft, even so much as a blade of grass."

If a śikṣamāṇā takes five coins or more than five coins—whether she takes it herself or instructs another to take it, whether she cuts it herself or instructs another to cut it, whether she breaks it herself or instructs another to break it, or whether she burns it, processes it, or alters its color—she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā;
she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
If one takes less than five coins, one commits an offense and should receive the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit such an offense; can you uphold it?
Respond by saying:
Yes. One must not intentionally take the life of any living being, even as small as an ant.

If a śikṣamāṇā intentionally takes a human life with her own hand, or seeks out a knife and gives it to another, or instructs another to die, encourages death, or praises death; or if she administers non-medicinal substances to another, causes an abortion, or performs incantations and sorcery herself or teaches others to do so; [she commits a grave offense].
She is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan.
If she has taken the life of an animal that cannot undergo transformation, she has violated the precepts and must be given the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit any transgression.
Can you uphold this? He replies: "I can."
One must not speak falsely, even in jest.

If a śikṣamāṇā, being untrue and having nothing [to claim], falsely declares to herself that she has attained the state of a superior person (uttarimanussa-dhamma), or that she has attained dhyāna, liberation, concentration, or meditative absorption, or that she has attained the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of an arhat, or that devas, nāgas, or yakṣas have come to make offerings to her—she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā;
she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
If one intentionally utters a falsehood within the assembly, one violates the precepts and should be given the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit such an offense; can you uphold this?
He replied: "I can.
I shall not eat at improper times."
If a śikṣamāṇā eats at an improper time, she commits an offense and must receive the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit such a transgression; can you uphold this?
He replied: "I can.
I shall not drink alcohol."
If a śikṣamāṇā drinks alcohol, she commits a violation of the precepts and must receive the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit this offense; can you maintain this?
She replies: [Yes].
Yes. A śikṣamāṇā should train in all the precepts of a bhikṣuṇī, with the exception of eating after noon.
Next, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the exhortation for the formal act (*karmavācanā*) should be stated as follows:
Listen, [Name]! The Saṃgha has already granted you the training rules.
A Śikṣamāṇā who undertakes and maintains the six rules is called a Śikṣamāṇā.

"You have obtained a complete and perfect Upādhyāyī, a complete and perfect Ācāryā, and a complete Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha; you have obtained a complete place of practice, a complete land, and the vow of a Cakravartin King—all these you have now fulfilled."
One should revere the Three Jewels—
the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel— as well as one’s preceptor-ni and teacher-ni, and show respect to those of the senior, middle, and junior seats.
One should diligently practice the three trainings:
the training in virtuous ethical discipline, the training in virtuous concentration, and the training in virtuous wisdom.
One should cultivate the three gates of liberation:
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
You should diligently apply yourself to the three activities:
sitting in meditation, reciting the scriptures, and exhorting others to perform meritorious deeds.
These dharmas open the gate to Nirvana, whereby one attains the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat.
Just as a lotus flower in the water grows and blossoms day by day, so too shall you grow in the Dharma of the Path; later, you shall receive full ordination.
Next, a verse is spoken:

"Within the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas, one has already obtained the precepts so difficult to find; since they are difficult to obtain even in times of no calamity, once obtained, do not let them go to waste."
He prostrated with his head at the feet of the Saṃgha, circumambulated them to the right, and departed with joy.
Regarding the ritual for requesting a *upādhyāyinī* (precept-giving nun) for the full ordination (*upasampadā*), one should speak as follows according to the formal procedure:
"Sister, attend to me with a single mind!"
I, [Name], now request the Venerable Nun to be my preceptor; may the Venerable Nun act as my preceptor.
By relying upon the Venerable Nun, I shall receive the full ordination.
He said this three times.
[The other] replied: "So be it."
The method for requesting the Precept Master (Śikṣamāṇā-ācāryā) according to the ritual protocol is as follows:
"Sister, please attend to me with a single mind!
I, [Name], now request you, Venerable Lady, to serve as my *karmavācanā* preceptor (*ācārya*). May you, Venerable Lady, act as my *karmavācanā* preceptor."
"By relying on you, my *ācāryā*, I have received the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
(Recite this three times. She replies:
"Very well. Please, Preceptor, perform the ritual according to the proper procedure and speak as follows:
'Sister, attend to me with a single mind!'"
I, [Name], now request the Venerable Nun to serve as my Preceptor for Instruction; may the Venerable Nun act as my Preceptor for Instruction.
It is by relying upon the Venerable Nun that I shall receive the Higher Ordination.
He said this three times.
[The other] replied: "So be it."
Regarding the procedure for establishing the location of one receiving the precepts: it should be established in a place where they are within sight but beyond hearing.
If the person receiving the precepts is in the open air, or hidden, or outside the range of sight and hearing, or outside the boundary, it is not termed "receiving full ordination."
The same applies to the *upādhyāyī* and the *bhikṣuṇīs* who complete the quorum.
Regarding the procedure for appointing a teacher of instruction (*śikṣācārya*), the preceptor (*śīlācārya*) asks within the assembly:
"Who among you is able to act as the teacher of instruction for that such-and-such person?"
If one acts as the preceptor, they should immediately reply:
"I, [Name], am able.
Having replied, the preceptor should make the following announcement:
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so.
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to grant its consent, let so-and-so serve as the instructor.
The announcement is thus made.
The instructor who has gone there to inquire about the impediments proceeds to the place where the candidate for ordination is and says:
"This is the *antarvāsa*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, the *saṃghāṭī*; this is the *saṃkakṣikā* and the *kaṭhina*."
"Is this your robe and bowl?
After he has replied, "It is," one should further say to him:
"Listen attentively!"
Now is the time for truthfulness; I now ask you: if it is so, say "it is"; if it is not, you should say "it is not.
Have you not committed a border offense?
Have you not violated a bhikṣu?
"Are you not one who has entered the Way with a thieving mind?
Are you not one who has broken away from the inner or outer paths? Are you not a eunuch?"
Have you not killed your father?
Have you not killed your mother?
Have you not killed an Arhat?
Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Have you not, with an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha?
Are you not a non-human being?
Are you not an animal? Are you not of dual gender? What is your name?
What is the name of the preceptor nun?
Has your age reached the required number?
Are your robes and alms bowl complete?
"Do your parents and husband permit you?
Are you not indebted to others?
Are you not a slave?"
Are you a woman? Women have such various ailments as leprosy,
white leprosy, abscesses, consumption, insanity, the confluence of the two channels, a narrow vaginal canal, constant leakage of urine and feces, and constant discharge of mucus and saliva.
"Do you have any such illnesses as these?
If he answers "No" to each question according to the facts, one should further say to him:
"As I have just asked, so shall the Sangha also ask you."
Just as you have answered me previously, so too should one answer within the Saṃgha.

Having finished the questioning, the instructor returns to the midst of the Saṃgha and, maintaining his usual dignified demeanor, stands at a distance where he can reach others with his outstretched arms and makes the following announcement:
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This person, [Name], seeks to receive the full ordination from the Preceptor Nun [Name].
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, I have finished instructing her; please allow her to come forward.
The formal motion is as follows: "Thus it is announced. He should then request the precepts from the Sangha, and they should say to him, "Come here.
Once he has come, they should have him take up his robes and bowl and instruct him to pay homage to the Sangha.
Having completed the ritual prostrations, he kneels long before the precept master with palms joined and speaks as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
I, [Name], seek to receive the full ordination from the Precept Master Nun [Name]."
I, [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the conferral of the full ordination, with the Bhikṣuṇī [Name] as my preceptor.
May the Saṃgha rescue me out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.)

If the person receiving the precepts does not state their own name, does not state the name of the precept-giving *upādhyāyī*, fails to request the precepts when instructed to do so, wears secular clothing, or is asleep, intoxicated, insane, naked, angry, unconscious, physically deformed, using another’s robes and bowl, lacks a *upādhyāyī*, has multiple *upādhyāyīs*, or if the assembly of monks is incomplete—in all such cases, it is not called "receiving the precepts."
The Preceptor’s Announcement: The Preceptor wishes to question [the candidate]; first, he makes this announcement. He announces:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen! May the Sangha hear me!"
This person, [Name], seeks to receive the full ordination from the Preceptor Nun [Name].
This person, [Name], now requests the Sangha to grant them the full ordination, with [Name] as their Preceptor Nun.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall ask about the various obstacles.
Thus is the formal announcement.
Having thus made the formal announcement regarding the method of questioning, the Preceptor says:
Listen attentively!
Now is the time for truth, the time for honest speech. I now ask you: if there is [something], you should say there is; if there is not, you should say there is not.
Have you not committed a bordering offense?
Have you not committed an offense against a bhikṣu?
Have you not entered the path with a thieving mind?
Have you not broken away from either the inner or outer paths?
Are you not a eunuch? Are you not one who has killed his father?
Are you not one who has killed his mother?
Have you not killed an Arhat?
Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Have you not, with malicious intent, shed the blood of a Buddha?
Are you not a non-human? Are you not an animal?
Are you not of both sexes?
"What is your name? What is the name of your preceptress (upādhyāyī)?
Have you reached the required age?"
Are your robes and alms bowl complete?
Have your parents and husband given you their permission?
Are you not indebted to anyone?
Are you not a slave?
Are you a woman? Women have such various ailments as these:

Leprosy, white leprosy, carbuncles, consumption, insanity, the fusion of the two channels, narrowness of the channels, constant leakage of urine and feces, and constant discharge of nasal mucus and saliva.
"Do you have any such illnesses?
Furthermore, according to the specific circumstances, one must answer "No" to each question.

To formally confer the fundamental rite, one should guide them with the Dharma, causing them to give rise to the highest grade of resolve and receive it with utmost sincerity; it should be performed in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so.
This person, so-and-so, now requests the Saṃgha for the full ordination, with the preceptor nun, so-and-so.
So-and-so declares herself pure, free from obstacles, twenty years of age, and fully equipped with robes and bowl.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant permission to confer the full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as her preceptor-ni.
The motion is thus made.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This person, [Name], seeks to receive the full ordination from the Preceptor Nun [Name].
This person, [Name], now requests from the Saṃgha the reception of the full ordination, with the Bhikṣuṇī [Name] as preceptor.
This person has declared herself pure; she is free from all obstacles, is twenty years of age, and is fully provided with robes and bowl.
The Sangha now confers the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptress-ni.
Those of you, sisters, who consent to the Sangha conferring the full ordination upon [Name] with [Name] as the preceptress-ni, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The motion has been stated three times.
The Saṃgha has already granted its consent for [Name] to receive the full ordination, with [Name] as the preceptress-ni.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The Method for Requesting the Karmācārya to Confer the Higher Ordination upon a Śrāmaṇerikā: The candidate for ordination, together with the community of bhikṣuṇīs, proceeds to the midst of the community of bhikṣus and, performing the ritual gestures before the ācārya, makes this request:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!"

I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to serve as my *karmācārya*. May the Venerable One act as my *karmācārya* out of compassion, so that by relying upon the Venerable One, I may receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
After it has been said three times, he should reply: "So be it."
Regarding the method for requesting ordination: after he has prostrated before the Saṃgha and performed the formal ritual, he should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, [Name], am seeking to receive the full ordination from the Preceptor Nun [Name]."
I, [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the conferral of the full ordination, with the Bhikṣuṇī [Name] as my preceptor.
May the Saṃgha rescue me out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.)
The Procedure for the Preceptor’s Announcement: In this rite, the preceptor first makes an announcement and subsequently asks questions. The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
This [person], so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so.
This [person], so-and-so, now requests the Sangha to grant her the full ordination, with the preceptor nun, so-and-so, acting as her preceptor.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, I shall inquire about the various obstacles.
Thus is the formal announcement.
Having thus announced the procedure for the Preceptor to inquire about the Dharma, he says:
Listen attentively!
Now is the time for truth, the time for honest speech. I now ask you: if there is something, you should say there is; if there is nothing, you should say there is not.
Have you not committed a pārājika offense?
Have you not committed an offense against a bhikṣu?
Are you not one who has taken up the path with a thief’s intent?
Are you not one who has broken away from the inner or outer paths?
Are you not a eunuch? Are you not one who has killed his father?
Are you not one who has killed his mother?
Have you not killed an Arhat?
Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Have you not, with a malicious mind, shed the blood of a Buddha?
Are you not a non-human? Are you not an animal?
Are you not of both sexes?
"What is your name? What is the name of your preceptress?
Have you reached the required age?"
Are your robes and alms bowl complete?
Have your parents or husband given you permission?
Are you not in debt to anyone?
Are you not a slave?
Are you a woman? Women have such various ailments as these:

Leprosy, white leprosy, carbuncles, consumption, insanity, the confluence of the two channels, narrowness of the channels, constant leakage of urine and feces, and constant discharge of mucus and saliva.
"Do you have any such illnesses?
If he answers "No" according to the facts, one should further ask:
"Have you studied the precepts?"
One should immediately reply:
"I have trained in the precepts.
One should then ask again:
"Are you pure? One should then answer: "I am pure."
Furthermore, one should ask the other nuns:
"Has so-and-so already studied the precepts?
The other nuns should reply:
Having already learned the precepts,
he is asked again:
"Are you pure?"
He answers again, saying:
"Pure. Once the preparatory procedures for the formal conferral of the precepts are complete, he instructs him as previously explained to receive them with full attention.
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This [person], so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so."
This person, [Name], now requests from the Saṃgha the reception of the full precepts, with the Bhikṣuṇī [Name] as her preceptor.
This person has declared herself pure; she is free from all obstacles, her age is complete, her robes and bowl are fully provided, and she has already trained in the purity of the precepts.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now confer the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor nun.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This [person], so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so.
This [person], so-and-so, now requests the Sangha to grant her the full ordination, with the preceptor nun, so-and-so, acting as her preceptor.
So-and-so has declared herself pure, free from obstacles, of full age, complete with robes and bowl, and having trained in the purity of the precepts.
The Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon So-and-so, with the Bhikṣuṇī So-and-so as her preceptor.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha conferring the full ordination upon [Name] with [Name] as the preceptor nun, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
This is said three times."
The Sangha has already consented; the full ordination for [Name] has been completed with [Name] as the preceptress-ni.
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya states:
"She declares herself pure and states that she has reached twenty years of age; the Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon [Name].
Since both parties recite these words, there is no error in following this recitation.
Having performed this rite, one should announce the time.
Receiving it from a border region is no different from this.
Regarding the ritual for conferring the characteristics of the precepts, one should say to that person:
Listen attentively, virtuous woman!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has proclaimed the eight pārājika rules; if a bhikṣuṇī violates them, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
One must not engage in impure conduct or practice the dharma of sexual desire.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in impure conduct or practices the dharma of sexual desire, even with an animal, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī;
she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not steal even so much as a blade of grass or a leaf.

If a bhikṣuṇī takes five coins or more than five coins from another person—whether she takes it herself or instructs another to take it; whether she cuts it herself or instructs another to cut it; whether she breaks it herself or instructs another to break it;
or whether she burns it, buries it, or destroys its color—she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not take the life of any living being, even down to an ant.

If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes a human life with her own hand, provides a weapon to another, instructs someone to die, praises death, encourages death, gives another a non-medicinal substance, causes an abortion, or employs incantations and sorcery;
or if she herself creates the means for it or instructs another to do so—she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you maintain it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not utter false speech, even in jest.
