If a bhikṣuṇī, being untrue and possessing nothing herself, claims to have attained the state of a superior person—saying she has attained dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, or meditative absorption (samāpatti), or that she has attained the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat, or that devas, nāgas, and spirits come to make offerings to her—she is not a bhikṣuṇī;
she is not a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not engage in physical contact, even with an animal.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, engages in physical contact with a man who has a defiled mind—anywhere from below the armpits to above the knees—whether by rubbing, pressing, stroking upward, stroking downward, pulling, pushing, lifting up, lowering down, grasping, or pressing firmly;
she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you maintain it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not commit these eight acts, even with an animal.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, accepts the hand-grasping, the robe-grasping, entering a secluded place, standing together in a secluded place, conversing together, walking together, physical leaning against one another, or making an appointment with a man who has a defiled mind;
if she commits these eight acts, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not conceal the grave offenses of others, even down to a *duṣkṛta* or an evil speech.
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a *pārājika* offense, she must not fail to report it herself, nor inform the Saṃgha, nor speak to others so that they may know.
At a later time, if this bhikṣuṇī has abandoned the path, or been expelled, or been barred from participating in the affairs of the Saṃgha, or has entered a non-Buddhist sect;
she then says: "I previously knew that this person had committed such and such an offense."
"She is not a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan, because she conceals another's grave offense.
You must not commit this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?"
He replied, "I can. [The Buddha said:
"One must not follow the words of a monk who has been suspended, nor even those of a śrāmaṇera."

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a bhikṣu has been formally charged by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions, for an offense against proper conduct (*ācāra*), and that he has not yet repented or performed the ritual of co-residence (*sāṃvāsika*),
yet she nevertheless follows the words of that bhikṣu.
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Sister!

That bhikṣu has been formally charged by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instruction; he has violated the rules of decorum and, having not yet confessed his offense, is not permitted to dwell in communal residence."
"Do not comply with the words of that bhikṣuṇī.
When the other bhikṣuṇīs admonish this bhikṣuṇī, if she persists and does not relinquish her position,
those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her up to three times so that she may abandon this matter.
Up to three admonitions, it is well if she relinquishes [the offense];
if she does not relinquish it, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan, because she has committed the offense of following the formal accusation.
You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can.
"Listen attentively, virtuous woman!"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has spoken four similes.

If one commits the eight offenses, it is like severing a person’s head so that they can never rise again; like cutting the heart of a tāla tree so that it no longer grows; like breaking the eye of a needle so that it can never be used again; like splitting a great stone into two parts so that they can never be joined back together.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits the eight grave offenses, she can no longer restore her status as a bhikṣuṇī.
"You must not violate these throughout the remainder of your life.
The four reliances should be conferred upon them as follows:
'Listen attentively, virtuous woman!'"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four reliances; it is the rule for bhikṣuṇīs that they rely upon these when going forth and receiving full ordination.
To go forth and receive full ordination by relying on rag-robes is the rule for bhikṣuṇīs.
Can you maintain this throughout your entire life?
Answer: Yes.
It is permissible.
If one obtains long-term benefits—
such as robes offered by a donor or robes made of cut-and-sewn cloth— one should accept them.
"Living by alms-seeking, leaving the household life, and receiving the full ordination—this is the Dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?
She replies:
Yes. If one obtains long-term benefits—

whether it be food assigned by the Saṃgha, food sent by a donor, food on the eighth day of the month, food on the fifteenth day, food on the first day of the month, the regular food of the community of monks, or food offered at a donor’s invitation— one should accept it.
"Taking up residence by sitting under a tree and receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*)—is this the law for bhikṣuṇīs? Can you maintain it for as long as life lasts?
She replies: "I can."
If one obtains long-term benefits—

This is stated three times.
One should not go solely for the sake of food and drink.
The formal ritual (karmavācanā) is performed on the grounds that the destination is so remote that one will not be able to return within seven days.
The Buddha said:

"I allow such a matter: one may receive the *saptāha-vidhi* (the rule for seven days), or the *pañcadaśāha* or *māsika-vidhi* (the rules for fifteen days or one month) through a formal motion and second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
It should be performed in this manner."
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant permission, let this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so receive the seven-day rule—extending to fifteen days or one month—to go outside the boundary for a certain purpose, and then return here to observe the rains retreat.
The announcement is as follows:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
The bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has received the seven-day, fifteen-day, or one-month leave of absence; she shall go outside the boundary for a certain purpose and return here to observe the rains retreat."

"Whichever sisters among you approve and grant their consent for the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to receive the 'seven-day-at-most' authorization to go outside the boundary for fifteen days or one month for a certain purpose, and then return to this very place for the rains retreat—those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve may speak."

The Sangha has already granted its consent for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to receive the seven-day, fifteen-day, or one-month *anujñā* (authorization) to go outside the boundary for a certain purpose, and having returned here, she shall complete her rains retreat within these limits.
The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent; thus this matter is upheld.

**Chapter 8: On the Invitation (Pravāraṇā)** **Part One: The Method for Appointing a Bhikṣuṇī to Go Before the Bhikṣu Saṃgha to Make the Pravāraṇā.** The World-Honored One permitted that when the bhikṣuṇīs have completed their summer retreat (*varṣā*), they should go before the bhikṣu saṃgha and perform the *pravāraṇā* regarding three matters:
what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
The formal motion and second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for appointing one bhikṣuṇī to go [to the assembly] should be carried out as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant permission, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to go into the midst of the great assembly for the sake of the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha."
"I announce the three matters of self-indulgence regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Thus it is announced.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to go before the Mahāsaṃgha on behalf of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha to announce the three matters for the Prātimokṣa.
"Regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected:

Whichever sisters approve of the Saṃgha appointing the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to go before the community of bhikṣus on behalf of the community of bhikṣuṇīs to announce the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*) concerning these three matters—what is seen, heard, or suspected—let her remain silent; whoever does not approve, let her speak."
The Saṃgha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to go before the community of bhikṣus on behalf of the community of bhikṣuṇīs to announce the three matters of self-examination:
what has been seen, heard, and suspected. This is concluded.
The Saṃgha consents by its silence; thus this matter is so upheld.
Since she travels alone without protection, it is permitted for the sake of her protection that two or three bhikṣuṇīs should be appointed as companions.

The procedure for a bhikṣuṇī to announce the *pravāraṇā* to the Saṃgha is as follows: This bhikṣuṇī goes into the midst of the bhikṣu-saṃgha; having prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, she bends her body, lowers her head, joins her palms, and speaks thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
The community of bhikṣuṇīs at [place name] has completed the summer rains retreat, and the community of bhikṣus has also completed the summer rains retreat.
The community of bhikṣuṇīs shall perform the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) regarding three matters:
what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
"Venerable ones, out of compassion, please speak to me; if I see my transgression, I shall confess it according to the Dharma.
This is said three times.

After this bhikṣuṇī has prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, she returns to her own monastery, strikes the wooden gavel to assemble the community of bhikṣuṇīs, and for those who do not come, she arranges for them to be represented by proxy, then addresses the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Venerable Sangha, you do not see any offense in the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha that can be raised based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Speak thus to the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha: 'Perform the *pravāraṇā* according to the Dharma; be diligent and do not be negligent!'"
When this announcement was made, the community of nuns all joined their palms and said:
"We shall receive and uphold it.
If the community of nuns has performed the *pravāraṇā* on that very day and is utterly exhausted, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* on the following day.
If the two assemblies are ill, incomplete, or discordant, one should dispatch a messenger to inquire after their welfare;
if one does not do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the procedure for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) to the Saṃgha: from this time forward, it is permitted to perform the *pravāraṇā* once the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) has concluded.
Regarding the request for permission to withhold the *pravāraṇā*: one should not seek such permission. Why?
Because the *pravāraṇā* itself is the granting of permission.
Furthermore, it is because they do not know that the *pravāraṇā* takes place today.
"Is it the time for the *pravāraṇā* tomorrow?
The Buddha said:
"If it is during the morning meal or the midday meal, the senior monk (*sthavira*) shall announce:"
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
Today, on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month at such-and-such a time, the Sangha assembles at such-and-such a place for the *pravāraṇā*.
All other ritual procedures and so forth are identical to those for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
Regarding the legal procedure for appointing those who receive the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults):

the Vinaya states that one is permitted to appoint such persons by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation), provided they are not partial, not angry, not afraid, and not deluded, and are able to distinguish whether the *pravāraṇā* has been performed or not yet performed.
The appointment should be made as follows:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

If the time has come for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to grant its consent, let the Sangha appoint the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to act as the recipient of the invitation to self-examination (pravāraṇā)."
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
The Sangha appoints the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to act as the recipient of the invitation to admonish."

"Whichever sisters approve of the Saṃgha's appointment of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as the one to receive the invitation to confess faults (pravāraṇā-grāhikā), let them remain silent; whichever do not approve, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has already approved and completed the appointment of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as the one to receive the invitation to confess faults."
The Saṃgha remains silent; therefore, this matter is thus upheld. Regarding the formal motion for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults), the Vinaya states:
"One should ask the person sitting nearby whether they have arrived or not."
First, make the formal announcement (jñapti), and afterwards perform the *pravāraṇā*. Make the announcement as follows:
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!..."
Today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen; let the Saṃgha perform the *pravāraṇā* in harmony.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Regarding the legal rules for the *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation) of the Saṃgha, it is said:
"One should be permitted to recite the invitation three times at a leisurely pace, ensuring that the *pravāraṇā* is clearly understood.
One must not wear the robe folded over the shoulders or wrapped around the neck; rather, one should expose one shoulder, etc."
She speaks as follows: "Sister!
Today the Saṃgha holds the Pravāraṇā ceremony; I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], also perform the Pravāraṇā."
If you see, hear of, or suspect a transgression, Sister, please speak to me out of compassion; if I see the transgression, I shall confess it according to the Dharma.
(Recite this three times.)
If a sick bhikṣuṇī is ill, the Buddha permits her to perform the *pravāraṇā* according to her own convenience.
The procedure for announcing purity (*śuddhi*) and the ritual method are identical to those for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
Regarding the abbreviated *pravāraṇā*, the Vinaya rules state:
If there are the eight difficulties or other circumstances, a brief *pravāraṇā* is permitted.
If the difficult situation is still far off and it is possible to speak at length, one should speak at length.
If the difficult situation is imminent and the threefold recitation cannot be performed, one should recite it twice.
If it is not possible to speak a second time, one should speak only once;
if not, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If the emergency is imminent and one cannot speak even once, one should immediately make a formal announcement (jñapti):
Each shall perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) by means of three statements, making the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now perform the *pravāraṇā* by means of three statements for each."
The announcement is made thus.
Having made this announcement, each person together performs the *pravāraṇā* with three statements;
the same applies to two statements or one statement.

If difficult circumstances are imminent, one may not perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) by means of three statements individually, nor may one make a formal announcement; rather, one should depart from the assembly on account of those matters.
Regarding the method of *pravāraṇā* performed face-to-face: if there are four persons, each should face the others and speak as follows:
"Three sisters, please bear this in mind!"
Today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, am pure regarding the *pravāraṇā*.
(Recite this) three times.
If there are three or two [bhikṣuṇīs], it is also done in this same manner.
The Method for Mindful *Pravāraṇā*: If there is but one person, she should mindfully reflect, saying:
"Today the Saṃgha performs *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, am pure regarding *pravāraṇā*."
The third recitation:

Regarding the method for extending the *pravāraṇā*, if there are many bhikṣuṇīs who have entered the rains retreat and diligently practice the Path, they may attain the realization of superior fruits.
They formed this thought:
"If we perform the *pravāraṇā* today, we shall have to move to another location, and we fear we may not obtain such happiness again.
Those bhikṣuṇīs then made a formal motion (*jñapti*) to extend the *pravāraṇā*.
Make the following announcement:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

If the time has come for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to grant its consent, the Sangha shall not perform the *pravāraṇā* today; when the four months are complete, it shall perform the *pravāraṇā*."
The announcement is made thus.
Having made this announcement, one proceeds until the full four months for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults).
Regarding the legal rules for increasing or decreasing the *pravāraṇā*, it is said:

If, on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, one hears that bhikṣuṇīs from another residence who are quarreling and discordant intend to come here for the *pravāraṇā*, those bhikṣuṇīs should perform the *pravāraṇā* by reducing the number of days by two or three.

If, after hearing [the announcement], they have already entered the boundary, one should provide them with bathing equipment and other necessities; having settled them, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* outside the boundary.
If they can act through such skillful means, it is well;
if they cannot, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* by means of a formal motion (*jñapti*) for the sake of the presiding authority.
He makes this formal announcement:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

If the time has come for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to grant its consent, let the Sangha not perform the *pravāraṇā* today, but rather perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight."
The motion is made thus.
Having made this motion, the *pravāraṇā* is further extended.
If visiting bhikṣuṇīs arrive during the dark fortnight, the resident bhikṣuṇīs should perform the second further extension of the *pravāraṇā* by means of a formal motion.
He should make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, the Saṃgha shall not perform the *pravāraṇā* today; rather, it shall perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the latter half of the month."
The announcement is made thus.
If the visiting bhikṣuṇīs still do not depart, the resident bhikṣuṇīs should, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, forcibly perform the *pravāraṇā* in harmony.
Chapter Nine: On the Acceptance and Purification of Robes, Alms Bowls, and Medicines (Part One). Regarding the method for accepting the five robes, according to the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*:
"Sister, attend closely with a single mind! [Recite as follows...]"
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], receive this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] strips; it is [length] long and [width] wide, a robe made of cut pieces, which I shall maintain.
(Recite three times.)
The procedure for receiving the next two robes is to be understood by analogy in the same way.
When receiving the *saṃkakṣikā* (shoulder-covering robe), one should say:
"Sister, please attend to me with a single mind!"
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], receive this shoulder-covering robe; it is four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width. This shoulder-covering robe I shall maintain.
(Recite three times.)
Receiving the *kūrmāra* robe, she says:
"Sister, attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [name], am receiving this *kūrmāra* robe; it is four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width. I shall maintain this *kūrmāra* robe."
Recite this three times.
The ritual for relinquishing the five robes should be performed by reversing the formula for receiving them, as follows:
"Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!"
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], having received this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] strips—[number] long and [number] short—as a robe made of cut pieces, now relinquish it.
Recite this three times.
The following four cases should be understood by analogy, each being the reverse [of the preceding].
The ritual for receiving the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) should be stated as follows:
Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], accept this niṣīdana as my auxiliary robe for the body.
(Recite three times.)
The method for receiving other auxiliary robes is the same as this rule.
One should know that the procedure for relinquishing them is the reverse of receiving them.
Regarding the legal rules for receiving the alms bowl (*pātra*):
There are two kinds of bowls:
first, those made of clay; second, those made of iron.
Their colors are likewise of two kinds:
The first is red, the second is black.
The large ones are three *dou* in capacity, the small ones are one and a half *sheng*.
These should be kept or given as pure gifts (*viśuddha-dāna*). Regarding their maintenance, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says:
Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], accept this pātra of standard measure for the purpose of long-term use.
(Recite three times.)
Regarding relinquishment, it should be understood as the opposite of receiving.
Regarding the legal rule for receiving sixteen vessels, the Vinaya states:
"If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a vessel on a given day, she should receive it on that very same day."
Of these, sixteen should be kept for use; the remainder should be given as pure gifts (śuddhadāna) or bestowed upon others.
As for the sixteen: there are large cauldrons with their lids, and small cauldrons likewise;
water jars with their lids, and rinsing jars likewise.
There are four basins and two ladles, one small and one large.
The recipient says:
"Sister, please attend to me with single-mindedness!"
"I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], this [vessel], numbered as the sixteenth among my set, I now receive.
(Recite three times).
Regarding the legal procedure for receiving non-timely medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*), the Vinaya states:
It is permitted to drink eight kinds of juices:
first, pear juice; second, rose-apple juice; third, jujube juice; fourth, sugarcane juice; fifth, *mṛdvīkā* juice; sixth, *śāluka* juice; seventh, *pāruṣaka* juice; and eighth, grape juice.
If it does not intoxicate people, one may drink it at improper times;
if it intoxicates people, one should not drink it, and if one drinks it,
one shall be dealt with according to the law.
One should first receive it from the hands of a pure person, and then address a bhikṣuṇī according to the Dharma, saying:
"Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!

I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], because of the circumstance of a certain illness, have this [Name] non-time juice; for the purpose of consuming it outside of the proper time, I now receive it from you, Sister."
Recite this three times.
The method for receiving the other two medicines is the same.
For the seven-day medicine, one should say:
Because it is for consumption over a period of seven nights while staying together,
one should say: "For long-term consumption while staying together for as long as life lasts."
Seven-day medicines are those such as clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Life-long medicines are all salty substances, fermented acids, and so forth, which are unfit to be used as food.
Regarding the ritual of "true purification" (*satya-pariśuddhi*), one should say:
Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I have this long robe which has not yet been purified; now, for the sake of purification, I relinquish it to you, Sister, for the purpose of true purification.
To perform the purification by truth (*bhūta-śuddhi*), one should inquire of the donor and only then may it be worn.
The same applies to the alms bowl, medicines, and the sixteen items.
Regarding the method of purification through succession (*paramparā-śuddhi*), one should say:
Sister, attend to me with one-pointed mind!
This is my extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) which has not yet been purified; for the sake of purification, I give it to you, Sister, so that it may be purified through transference.
The recipient who accepts the purification should say:
"Sister! You have this extra robe which has not yet been purified; for the sake of purifying it, give it to me, and I shall now accept it.
Having accepted it, he says:
"To whom did you give it?
He should reply: "I gave it to so-and-so."
The recipient of the purification says: "Sister!
This is an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) which you have not yet purified; for the sake of purifying it, you give it to me, and I now accept it."
Having received it, you give it to [Name]; this robe now belongs to [Name]. You must guard and maintain it well for [Name], wearing it according to the circumstances.
Having been passed down through a pure act of giving (*pariṣkāra-dāna*), whether [Name] asks or does not ask, you are permitted to wear it as you please.
The procedures for the alms bowl, medicine, and the sixteen items are likewise the same; the only difference lies in the specific designation of the objects.

Regarding the timing for present offerings, the Vinaya states:
From this day forward, one should not seek summer robes at any time during spring, summer, or winter;
nor should one dwell in residence in one place while receiving one's share of summer robes from another.

Furthermore, there were those who, having entered the summer retreat at one residence, subsequently stayed at another location; they did not know from which place they should take their provisions for the retreat.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to take them from the place where one has stayed for the greater number of days."
"If both parties are equal, it is permitted for each to take half.
It is further stated:
"When the Saṃgha obtains robes for the summer retreat, the Saṃgha may be divided into two factions."
The Buddha said:
"One should divide it according to the number of people.
Whether the summer robes have not yet been received or have already been received, if the Saṃgha is split into two factions, one should likewise divide it by counting the number of people."
Regarding these cases where gifts are offered in person, there is no fixed rule for the distribution.
When receiving robes through the practice of accepting untimely gifts offered in person, if one does not know how to proceed, [the following applies].
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to divide it.
You should count the number of people and divide accordingly; if there are ten people, divide into ten portions, and so on up to a hundred people, which would be divided into a hundred portions."
When good and evil are mixed in their proportions,
one should not take the portion for oneself, but should have another person take it.
One should not cast the voting tally oneself, but should have someone who is out of sight cast the tally.
Since this involves several people, there is no method for individual allotment.

Regarding the procedure for distributing gifts given by the Saṃgha during the collection period: if lay devotees offer items for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), they should be divided according to the gift regardless of the specific location. If one has performed the labor of the *varṣā* at the place where the items were obtained, even if one’s body is not present, it is permitted to take possession of them through formal assignment (*parivāsa*).
The Vinaya states:
If a single bhikṣu observes the rains retreat and receives a large amount of requisites for the summer retreat from the Saṃgha, that bhikṣu should form this mental resolve:
"This is my property."

Regarding the *karmavācanā* ritual for the face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*), it is identical to the rules for the untimely distribution of gifts to the Saṃgha (*akālabhikṣā*) and differs in no other respect; therefore, they are not set forth here separately.

As for the method of appointing a distributor of items for the untimely distribution of gifts to the Saṃgha: if there is a monastery where the resident Saṃgha has obtained divisible clothing or property, [the following applies].
The Vinaya states:
"It is permitted to divide [the robes]. At the time of division, guests arrived one after another, and they became utterly exhausted from dividing the robes.
One person should be appointed to perform the distribution; this person must possess five qualities, which are as stated above.
It should be done in this manner:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to act as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha.
This is the motion.
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to act as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha.
Those of you, sisters, who consent to the appointment of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Distributing rice gruel for the Saṃgha, distributing morning snacks (*khajjaka*), hard foods (*khaajja-bhojana*), assigning invitations to assemblies, spreading bedding, distributing bedding, distributing bathing robes, giving, taking, and appointing bhikṣuṇīs as messengers—all such matters are likewise [to be performed by the *vaiyāpṛtyakara*].
There are five qualities by which one who distributes rice porridge for the Saṃgha goes to hell as swiftly as a shot arrow: namely, having craving and so forth.
There are five qualities by which one who distributes rice porridge is born in heaven as swiftly as a shot arrow: namely, being without craving and so forth.
The same applies even to the appointment of a śrāmaṇerī as a messenger.
Regarding the procedure for entrusting items for the distribution of robes: once the person has been appointed, the items must be entrusted to them.
The entrustment is performed in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
Whatever is here in this residence—whether robes or non-robes—the present Saṃgha should divide it.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now give this to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, who shall then give it to the Saṃgha.
The motion is thus stated.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
Whatever exists in this residence—whether it be robes or non-robes—the present Sangha should divide among themselves.
The Saṃgha now gives this to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, who shall in turn give it to the Saṃgha.

and that the Saṃgha gives it to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, who shall in turn give it to the Saṃgha: those who consent remain silent; whoever does not consent, please speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to grant [this] to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so; she shall now complete the granting to the Saṃgha.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Having performed this rite, it is to be distributed equally among the persons concerned.
If the śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs are in harmony, they shall receive an equal share;
if they are not in harmony, they shall receive one part out of two;
and if they are still not in harmony, they shall receive one part out of three.
Furthermore, if [the donor] does not give [it], it should not be divided.
For the monastery attendants, one-fourth is to be given;
if they do not give [it], it should not be divided.

The Procedure for Directly Taking Possession of Objects by Four Persons: If there are only four persons, it does not constitute a formal delegation; one should directly perform the act of taking possession.
It should be performed as follows:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!..."
Whatever is present at this dwelling, whether it be robes or non-robes, the *saṃgha* currently assembled should divide it.
If the time is right for the *saṃgha*, and the *saṃgha* grants its consent, let the *saṃgha* now divide these items among those present.

Regarding the legal rules for the property of a deceased bhikṣuṇī, the Vinaya states:

The monastery’s gardens, fields, and fruit trees were divided; furthermore, the cells and the belongings belonging to the individual cells were divided; furthermore, the bronze jars, bronze basins, cauldrons, and other heavy items were divided; furthermore, the rope beds, wooden beds, sitting mats, bedding, and pillows were divided; furthermore, the *elāyanta*, *morata*, *mora-mora*, and woolen rugs were divided; furthermore, the carriages and the monastery attendants were divided; furthermore, the water pitchers, wash-basins, mendicant staffs, and fans were divided; furthermore, the iron tools, wooden tools, ceramic tools, leather tools, and bamboo tools were divided.

Regarding the legal rules for rewarding those who tend to the sick, the Vinaya states:
The Sangha asks the attendant to say:

There are five qualities one should possess to be given property by a patient:
first, knowing what the patient may eat and what they may not eat, and being able to provide what they may eat;
second, not loathing or despising the patient’s excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit.
Third, possessing a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, one does not act for the sake of food or clothing;
fourth, being able to manage medical treatments until the patient recovers or passes away;
fifth, being able to preach the Dharma to the sick person, causing them to rejoice, while also increasing one’s own progress in wholesome dharmas.
If these five conditions are met, one may take the clothing and requisites of a sick person.
As for items such as their alms bowl, they should be given as a reward according to what is currently available;

11. Chapter on the Virtuous Robe (Middle). Chapter Eleven on the Virtuous Robe: The Formal Declaration for Receiving the *Kaṭhina* Cloth. The Vinaya states:
Whether it be a new robe, a robe offered by a donor, or a refuse rag—
whether it be a new garment or an old one— if it is a new item, one should mark it as pure;
if it has already been washed, one should wash it and then mark it as pure.
It must not be obtained through wrong livelihood, nor by means of signs, nor by agitation, nor by being kept overnight, nor by the rite of purification for an article subject to forfeiture.
It must be acquired on that very day in accordance with the Dharma; it should have a border sewn around the four edges and be made of five strips with ten sections.
Even if it exceeds these specifications, it may still be accepted.
One should personally wash, dye, stretch out, and press it flat, then cut it into ten sections and sew them together.
One should receive it before the community of monks, making the following announcement:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!"
Today the community of monks receives the *guṇa-vastra*.
If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, grant its consent that the community of monks, in harmony, shall receive the *guṇa-vastra*.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Regarding the appointment of a person to maintain the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit), the Vinaya states:
One should ask who is capable of maintaining the *guṇa-cīvara*.
If someone says they are capable, one should appoint them by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation).
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to hold the kaṭhina robe on behalf of the Saṃgha."
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
The Sangha appoints the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to hold the kaṭhina robe on behalf of the Sangha."
"Whichever sisters approve of appointing the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to hold the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has approved the appointment of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to hold the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha."
Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Having assigned the *kaṭhina* robe to the robe-holding official according to the prescribed rules, one performs the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to entrust it.
It should be done in this manner:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This dwelling-place has obtained clothing and other items that may be distributed; these should now be divided among the present members of the Saṃgha."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha now bestows this robe upon the bhikṣuṇī [Name]; this bhikṣuṇī shall take this robe and, on behalf of the Saṃgha, receive it as a *kaṭhina* robe and maintain it at this residence.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
This residence has obtained clothing and other items suitable for distribution; these should now be distributed among the present members of the Sangha."

The Sangha now bestows this robe upon the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so; this bhikṣuṇī shall take this robe for the Sangha to receive and make it into a kaṭhina robe, and she shall maintain it at this residence.
"Whichever sisters approve of the Saṃgha holding this robe to give it to such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī to receive and make into a *guṇa-cīvara*, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak."
The Saṃgha has already consented to give the robe to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the procedure for receiving the robe before the Saṃgha: the bhikṣuṇī who holds the robe should stand up and take hold of it; then, as the hands of the various bhikṣuṇīs reach the robe at the point where the verbal exchange is clear, she should speak as follows:

This robe the community of monks shall accept to make into a merit-robe; this robe the community of monks now accepts to make into a merit-robe; this robe the community of monks has already accepted and finished making into a merit-robe.
Recite this three times.
The bhikṣuṇīs should speak as follows:
"The recipient has properly received [the precepts]; whatever merit and renown exist herein belong to me."
The person holding the robes should reply,
"So be it. In this manner, the sequence continues down to the lowest seat.
Having received [the formal authorization], one is permitted to perform five things:

first, to keep extra robes; second, to stay overnight apart from one's robes; third, to eat in a separate group; fourth, to eat by successive invitations; and fifth, to enter a village without having informed a bhikṣuṇī.
Regarding the legal rules for appointing a person to make a *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe):
if unmade robes are obtained, the Saṃgha should appoint a person to make them by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement).
The appointment should be made in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to prepare the *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe) for the Saṃgha.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
The Sangha appoints the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to prepare a *kaṭhina* robe for the Sangha.
Those venerable sisters who consent to the appointment of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to prepare the *kaṭhina* robe for the Sangha should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to prepare the *guṇa-cīvara* for the Saṃgha.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The ritual procedure is as before.
Regarding the method for relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe: if one does not relinquish the *kaṭhina*, one should form this intention:
"I shall relinquish [the privileges] because the five benefits have been obtained for a long time."
The Buddha said:
"You should not entertain such thoughts. When the four months of winter have concluded, the Saṃgha should distribute the *kaṭhina* robe.
It should be done in this manner."
Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
Today the Sangha is to bring forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
If the time for the Sangha has come, and the Sangha is willing to grant its consent, let the Sangha now, in harmony, bring forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
The announcement is made thus.
If one does not relinquish the robe, and the period for the *kaṭhina* robe expires, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are eight causes and conditions by which the *kaṭhina* robe is relinquished:
1. Departure; 2. Completion; 3. Non-completion; 4. Loss; 5. Severance of hope; 6. Hearing; 7. Crossing the boundary; 8. Exiting together.
Furthermore, there are two ways in which the *kaṭhina* robe may be relinquished:
if a bhikṣuṇī who is wearing the *kaṭhina* robe spends the night outside the boundary, the Saṃgha, being in harmony, shall together relinquish it.

Chapter Twelve: Expiation of Offenses (Middle) Expiation of Offenses, Chapter Twelve Regarding the rules for expiating *pārājika* offenses, according to the Vinaya, there are five kinds of confession:
There may be those who commit an offense and repent through their own mental reflection;
there may be those who commit a minor offense and repent before another;
or there may be those who commit a middling offense and likewise repent before another.
There are those who commit grave offenses and repent before others;
there are also those whose offenses cannot be repented of—these irredeemable offenses are called *pārājika* offenses.
Regarding those who have committed a *pārājika* offense, there are three legal procedures:
first, for one who commits the offense and conceals it, the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) is administered;
second, for one who commits the offense and does not conceal it, the *yāvaj-jīvam-śikṣādattaka-karman* (act of lifelong training and repentance) is administered.
3. Regarding one who has committed a transgression while undergoing training for repentance (*śikṣādattaka*) and commits it again: the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) is to be performed.

If one who has concealed [the offense] is subjected to the rite of *pravāsanīya*, and if one who has concealed a *pārājika* offense, the Saṃgha shall first perform the act of formal accusation (*codanā*), the act of calling to mind (*smṛti*), and the imposition of the penalty.
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense."

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so for a certain *pārājika* offense; she shall not dwell together with the community, nor shall she engage in communal affairs.
The motion is thus:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense."

The Saṃgha now performs the formal act of *nihsargika-pācittiya* for the expulsion of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so for a certain *pārājika* offense; she shall not dwell together with them, nor shall she engage in communal affairs.

Those venerable sisters who consent to the Saṃgha’s performance of the formal act of expulsion for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so for a certain *pārājika* offense—granting that she shall not dwell together with them nor engage in communal affairs—should remain silent. Whoever does not consent should speak.
The motion has been stated three times.

The Sangha has already granted the formal act of *nihsargika-pārājika* expulsion for the nun so-and-so; she is not to dwell together with them, nor is she to engage in communal affairs. The procedure is concluded.
The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is upheld as such.
Regarding the legal rule for granting lifelong *śikṣā-dattaka* (probationary training) to one who has not concealed [the offense]:
if one has not yet committed a *pārājika*, one shall never commit one.

If she has already committed the offense but has no intention of concealment whatsoever and confesses according to the Dharma, it is permitted for the Saṃgha to grant her the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for the Pārājika precepts.
That bhikṣuṇī should perform the proper ritual within the Saṃgha and make this request as follows.
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; having no intention whatsoever to conceal it, I now beg the Saṃgha for the pārājika discipline.
"May the Saṃgha grant me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], the Pārājika precepts, out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.
The Saṃgha should grant the dharma in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This Bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; being without any intention to conceal it, she now requests from the Saṃgha the pārājika discipline.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, grant the Pārājika precepts now to this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; being without a mind of concealment, she now requests from the Saṃgha the pārājika discipline;
the Saṃgha now grants the pārājika discipline to this bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so.
"Whichever sisters approve of the Saṃgha bestowing the *pārājika* precept upon the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak.
This is asked three times.
The Saṃgha has approved and completed the bestowal of the *pārājika* precept upon the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so."
The Saṃgha consents, as they remain silent; thus this matter is upheld.
Having received the Pārājika precepts, one must follow and practice them accordingly throughout the duration of one's life.
One who practices in accordance with the Dharma:
may not confer the full ordination upon others;
may not provide dependence for others.
One must not keep a śrāmaṇerikā;
if appointed to go before the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha to request instruction and admonition, one must not accept;
even if appointed, one should not go.
One should not recite the precepts for the Saṃgha;
one should not engage in questions and answers regarding the Vinaya within the Saṃgha;
and one should not accept an appointment from the Saṃgha to serve as an administrator.
One should not accept the assignment of adjudicating legal matters for the Saṃgha;
one should not accept the mission of being dispatched on behalf of the Saṃgha;
and one should not enter a village too early or return at the close of day.
One should associate with bhikṣuṇīs;
one must not associate with followers of external paths or laypeople;
one should comply with the dharma of bhikṣuṇīs.
One must not speak other worldly speech;
one must not recite the Vinaya in the midst of the assembly, though it is permitted if there is no one else capable of reciting it;
one must not commit this offense again.
One should not commit other offenses either—whether they are similar, derived from this, or more serious than this;
one must not participate in a *karmavācanā* that is not performed by the Saṃgha, nor perform a *karmavācanā* oneself;

and one must not accept from a pure bhikṣuṇī the spreading of a sitting mat, water for washing the feet, wiping of leather sandals, rubbing or massaging the body, as well as prostrations, welcoming and seeing off, or inquiries after her welfare.
One should not accept the robes and bowl held by a pure bhikṣuṇī;
one must not raise a pure bhikṣuṇī to provide a reminder or to subject her to the *svavacanadaṇḍa* (punishment by self-accusation);
and one should not testify on behalf of a person who is upright.
One must not obstruct a pure bhikṣuṇī from reciting the precepts or performing the *pravāraṇā*;
one must not engage in dispute with a pure bhikṣuṇī.

Regarding a bhikṣuṇī who has committed a *pārājika* offense, whether she comes or does not come when the Saṃgha recites the precepts or performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*), the assembly incurs no offense.

Regarding the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (expulsion) for one who has committed a grave offense after having been granted the opportunity to repent: if one has already been granted the *pārājika* discipline and commits it again, they should be expelled.
The formal acts such as the *codanā* (reproval) and so forth should be performed in this manner.

This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; being without any intention to conceal it, she has already requested the pārājika penance from the Sangha, and the Sangha has already granted the pārājika penance to this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
While this bhikṣuṇī was undergoing the *śikṣāmanavatī* (probationary training), she has again committed a certain *pārājika* offense.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment) against this bhikṣuṇī for her repeated commission of a certain *pārājika* offense; she shall not dwell together [with the community] and shall not participate in communal affairs.
The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; being without a mind to conceal it, she has already requested from the Sangha the pārājika discipline."
The Saṃgha has already granted the *pārājika* discipline to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
While she was in the process of training for repentance, she again committed such-and-such a *pārājika* offense.

The Saṃgha now grants the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) for the repeated commission of such-and-such a *pārājika* offense to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so; she shall not dwell together [with the Saṃgha], nor shall she engage in communal affairs.

Whichever sisters among you approve of the Sangha’s formal act of banishment for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, who has repeatedly committed such-and-such a pārājika offense—depriving her of communal residence and communal affairs—remain silent; whoever does not approve, please speak.
The motion has been stated three times.

The Saṃgha has already granted the formal act of banishment for a nun who has repeatedly committed a pārājika offense, such that she shall not dwell together [with the community] and shall not participate in communal affairs. It is concluded.
The Saṃgha having consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
There are three kinds of formal acts (karmavācanā) for the removal of offenses involving residual transgression (saṃghāvaśeṣa):
first, the *mānatva* for half a month; [the second is the *āvarhaṇa*; the third is the *ābhṛti*].
Second, if one commits a heavy offense while practicing [the penance], one undergoes the *ardhamāsa-mūlāpakarṣa* (half-monthly reduction of the original period) and,
third, the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*). There are only two ways to attain the status of a *dharma-sthiti* (one established in the Dharma):
First, regarding those who have committed a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) after having already received the legal procedure (*karmavācanā*), there are three types of procedures;
second, regarding those who have not committed a grave offense after receiving the legal procedure, there are two types.

As for the procedure of the half-month *mānatva*: if one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, they should perform the *mānatva* for half a month within each of the two assemblies of the Saṃgha, with at least four monks present in each.
That bhikṣuṇī should go before the Saṃgha, kneel with her right knee on the ground, and make this request:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. I now request from the Saṃgha a half-month period of mānāpya."
"I pray that the Saṃgha grant me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], the half-month *mānatva*, out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.
The Saṃgha should grant the procedure in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, has committed a certain saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and now requests from the Saṃgha a half-month of *mānāpya*.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant it, let the Saṃgha grant this bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, a half-month of *mānāpya*.
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī [Name], having committed such-and-such a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, now requests from the Saṃgha a half-month of mānatva.
The Saṃgha grants a half-month *mānatva* penance to the bhikṣuṇī [Name].
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha granting a half-month *mānatva* penance to the bhikṣuṇī [Name], remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
This has been stated three times.
The Saṃgha has already granted the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so the half-month *mānatva* penance;
the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus this matter is upheld.

The Procedure for Informing the Saṃgha Regarding the Practice of *Mānatva*: Once he has received this dharma and wishes to practice it immediately, he should perform the formal ritual within the Saṃgha and make the following announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed a certain Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and have already requested from the Saṃgha a half-month of mānāpya;
the Saṃgha has already granted me, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], a half-month of mānāpya.
"I now perform the *mānatva* rite; may the Saṃgha bear this in mind.
This is recited three times.
Having made this formal announcement, one fully performs the "seven fives" practices; these seven fives have been explained above.
He goes to where pure bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs reside, performing for each one the duties of a disciple toward a preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
There are eight matters by which one loses the night (*rātriparihāṇi*):
first, going to another monastery without informing [the preceptor].
2. When visiting bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs arrive, one does not inform [the resident community];
3. When leaving the boundary for some business, one does not inform [the community];
4. When bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs walk slowly within the monastery, one does not inform [them].
5. Not sending a messenger to inform [the host] when ill;
6. Staying overnight in the same room with two or three people, excluding one's companions;
7. Residing in a place where there are neither bhikṣus nor bhikṣuṇīs.
Eighth, failing to announce [the assembly] when it is not the time for the fortnightly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*);
these are the eight matters by which the night is lost.
Should one violate even a single item, the night is lost and one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Each day, this bhikṣuṇī who is performing the *mānatva* penance within the Saṃgha must stay overnight among the Saṃgha and announce it daily.
At the time of the announcement, she should address the Saṃgha with the proper ritual form, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed a certain Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and have already requested from the Saṃgha a half-month period of mānāpya;
the Saṃgha has already granted me, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], a half-month period of mānāpya.

I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], am practicing *mānatva*; having already practiced it for several days and not yet having practiced it for several days, I inform the venerable Saṃgha so that they may know: "I am practicing *mānatva*."
If the *sūtra* mentions the proclamation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) or going to another monastery and so forth, one should know that these are largely the same.

Regarding the procedure for announcing the suspension of the observance: if the assembly is difficult to gather, if one does not wish to proceed, or if the person concerned is weak and possesses much shame, one should go before a pure bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī and, having performed the proper etiquette, announce:
"Venerable Sir" (if addressing a bhikṣu), or "Sister" (if addressing a bhikṣuṇī).
"I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], today relinquish the instruction not to perform [the formal act].

When one wishes to perform the procedure for relinquishing the formal act, one should go before a pure Bhikṣu or Bhikṣuṇī and, having prepared the proper decorum, say: 'Venerable Sir,' if addressing a Bhikṣu;
or 'Sister,' if addressing a Bhikṣuṇī."
"I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], today shall act according to the instructions given.
Having made this formal announcement (*jñapti*), she proceeds as previously described.
Regarding the procedure for concluding the *mānāpya* practice once it has been completed: once the practice is finished, she should immediately announce it to the Saṃgha.
Having come into the midst of the Saṃgha, she performs the formal ritual and says:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed a certain saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and have already requested from the Saṃgha a half-month period of mānatva."
"The Sangha has already granted me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], a half-month *mānatva*.
I have now completed the practice of this *mānatva*; may the Sangha remember and uphold this.
(Recite this three times.)"

Regarding the procedure for the *mānāpya* (probation) and the *pārivāsika-mūla-parivāsa* (re-initiation of probation): since he has committed a new offense while undergoing the former, he is granted the *mūla-parivāsa*.
He then proceeds to the Saṃgha and, having performed the formal ritual, makes this request.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed a certain saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and have already requested from the Saṃgha a half-month mānatva; the Saṃgha has already granted me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], a half-month mānatva.

I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], while practicing *mānatva*, have again committed a certain *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense during that interval. I now request from the Saṃgha the *mānatva* for half a month and the *mānatvāhvayakarman* for the original day regarding this previous offense and the subsequent re-offense of a certain *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], who previously committed and subsequently re-committed a certain saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, the half-month *mānatva* and the *mānatva* and *yadbhūyaḥ-karma* (the formal act of returning to the original status).
This is said three times.
The Sangha should grant the *dharma*.
Listen, venerable Sangha!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, having committed such-and-such a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, has already requested from the Saṃgha a half-month of mānāpya;
the Saṃgha has already granted this bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, a half-month of mānāpya.

This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, while practicing *mānatva*, has again committed a certain *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense during that interval. She now requests from the Saṃgha the *mānatva* for a half-month and the *mānatvāhar-āvarhaṇa-karman* (the formal act of resetting the *mānatva*) for her previous offense and this intermediate re-offense of a certain *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha confer upon the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so the *mānatva* for half a month and the *mānatva* and *yadbhūyaḥ-karma* for the intermediate reoffense of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense previously committed.
It is announced as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has committed a certain saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and has already requested from the Saṃgha a half-month period of mānāpya."
The Saṃgha has already granted this Bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, a half-month *mānāpya* for a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

While this Bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, was practicing the *mānāpya*, she again committed a further *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of the same kind during that interval. She now requests from the Saṃgha a half-month *mānāpya* and a *mānāpya-caritta-mūla-parivāsa-karman* for her previous offense and the subsequent offense committed during the interval.
The Saṃgha grants this Bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, a half-month *mānāpya* and a *mānāpya-caritta-mūla-parivāsa-karman* for her previous offense and the subsequent offense committed during the interval.

"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha granting this bhikṣuṇī—who previously committed [an offense] and subsequently committed a grave offense of the same kind—a half-month *mānatva* and the *mānatva* and *yadbhūyaḥkaraṇa* (reinstatement) *karmavācanā*, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak."
The motion has been stated three times.

The Sangha has granted the *mānatva* for half a month and the *mānatva* and *yadbhūyaḥ-karma* (the formal act of the day of *mānatva*) for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, who previously committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and subsequently committed it again with greater gravity; this is now concluded.
Since the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent, this matter is upheld as such.
The formal announcement (*jñapti*) and the performance of the disciplinary measures (*karma*) are the same as previously described; the procedure must be fully set forth in writing.

Regarding the method for conferring the *mānāpya* (probation) that is not subject to destruction and for the rite of absolution from offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*), there are two types of this rite of absolution:
First, the method for not breaking the *mānāpya*; second, the method for breaking the *mānāpya*.

When a bhikṣuṇī who follows the method for not breaking [the *mānāpya*] has completed her *mānāpya*, she should be absolved of the offense before two assemblies of the Saṃgha, each consisting of at least twenty members.
Having arrived among the Saṃgha, she performs the formal ritual and makes this request:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
I, the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and have already requested from the Saṃgha a half-month *mānatva*."

I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], having completed the practice of *mānatva*, now request from the Sangha the formal act for the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna-karman*).

The Saṃgha should then grant the legal procedure.

The motion is as follows:

The Saṃgha has also granted me, bhikṣuṇī [Name], the *mānatva* for half a month and the *mānatvābhisamācaraṇa-karman* for the previously committed and subsequently repeated *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.

I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], having committed a certain Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense during the course of my prior offense, have now completed the half-month *mānatva* and the *mānatva-mūla-parivāsa* karmavācanā. I now request from the Saṃgha the *āpattivyutthāna* (expiation) karmavācanā.
"May the Saṃgha grant me, the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, the formal act for the removal of offenses (āpattivyutthāna-karman), out of compassion.

The Saṃgha should then grant the procedure.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has committed a certain saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and has already requested from the Saṃgha a half-month of mānāpya;
the Saṃgha has already granted this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so a half-month of mānāpya.

While this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so was practicing *mānatva*, she again committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense during that interval. She has also requested from the Saṃgha the *mānatva* for half a month and the *mānatvāhar-aticaraṇa-karman* (the formal act of the day of *mānatva*) for her previous offense and the subsequent re-offense of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Saṃgha has also granted this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so the *mānatva* for half a month and the *mānatvāhar-aticaraṇa-karman* for her previous offense and the subsequent re-offense of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, having previously committed [a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense] and subsequently committing it again during the interval, has now completed the half-month *mānatva* and the *mānatva-parivāsa* and *mūla-parivāsa* karmans for that saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; she now requests from the Saṃgha the karma of rehabilitation (*āpattivyutthāna*).
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha absolve this bhikṣuṇī of her offense.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, having committed such-and-such a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, has already requested from the Saṃgha a half-month *mānatva*;
the Saṃgha has already granted this bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, a half-month *mānatva*.

While this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so was practicing *mānatva*, she again committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense during that interval. She has also requested from the Saṃgha the *mānatva* for half a month and the *mānatvāhar-āvarhaṇa-karman* (the formal act of returning to the original day) for the previously committed offense and the subsequently committed *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense during the interval;

the Saṃgha has likewise granted this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so the *mānatva* for half a month and the *mānatvāhar-āvarhaṇa-karman* for the previously committed offense and the subsequently committed *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense during the interval.

This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, having previously committed [a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense] and subsequently committing it again during the interval, has completed the half-month *mānatva* and the *mānatva-mūla-parivāsa* karmavācanā for the [offense of] such-and-such *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. She now requests from the Saṃgha the *āpattivyutthāna* (expiation) karmavācanā;
may the Saṃgha grant the *āpattivyutthāna* to this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
"Whichever elders approve of the Sangha granting the rehabilitation from offense to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak up.

"The Sangha has approved and completed the granting of rehabilitation from offense to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so."
The Saṃgha having consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the case of the *sthūlātyaya* offense, according to this [text], there are two categories of *sthūlātyaya*:
first, the fundamental (*mūla*); [second, the derivative].
Second, [the classification] according to origin.
Within these two, there are three grades of repentance.
The first is the superior grade, which is repentance before the great assembly; this refers to the root [offenses]:
For those who destroy the Wheel of Dharma, steal the four requisites, kill a deva, and so forth;
among the offenses arising from birth:
they range from *pārājika* down to heavy *sthūlātyaya*.
The second is the medium grade, which involves repentance before a small assembly;

this refers to the fundamental offenses, such as causing a schism in the *saṃgha* through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), being an associate in destroying the Wheel of Dharma, or stealing the three robes and so forth;
and those arising from birth:
Below *pārājika* is the light *sthūlātyaya*; below *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is the heavy *sthūlātyaya*.
Third is the inferior grade, which requires confession before a single person; this refers to those within the root [offenses]:
shaving hair, being naked, wearing human skin, using stone bowls, eating raw meat or blood, wearing the robes of non-Buddhists, stealing one *kārsāpaṇa*, and so forth.
Regarding the categories of offenses arising from birth: those lighter than *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are *sthūlātyaya*.
As for the method of confession before the Saṃgha, the aforementioned offense of a superior-grade *sthūlātyaya* must be confessed before the Saṃgha.
He goes before the Saṃgha, assumes the proper demeanor, and requests confession from the Saṃgha,
making this request: "Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!..."
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed such-and-such a sthūlātyaya offense. I now beg the Saṃgha for forgiveness through repentance.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], permission to repent.
This is stated three times.

Regarding the request for a master of confession (*pratideśanā-ācārya*): one who wishes to confess should, within the Saṃgha, request a pure bhikṣuṇī to serve as the master of confession. One must not confess to someone who has committed an offense, nor may one who has committed an offense accept another's confession; that bhikṣuṇī should go to the place of a pure bhikṣuṇī.
If the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense and no confession is possible, and if there are visiting bhikṣuṇīs who are pure and without offense, one should go to them to confess;
if no visiting bhikṣuṇīs arrive, then two or three people should be dispatched to a nearby community of pure practitioners to perform the confession.
This bhikṣuṇī shall return to her place of residence, and the bhikṣuṇīs residing there shall perform an act of repentance before this pure bhikṣuṇī.
Having assumed the proper demeanor, they shall make this request:
"Sister, please attend to us with one-pointed mind!
I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed such-and-such a sthūlātyaya offense. I now request the Venerable Sister to act as my witness for repentance.
May the Venerable Sister, out of compassion, act as my witness for repentance!
First, the procedure for the master of confession to inform the Saṃgha: the master of confession must not grant permission immediately; they must first inform the Saṃgha.
The announcement is made as follows:
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has committed a certain sthūlātyaya offense and now requests the Saṃgha for confession.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits it, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
The announcement is made as follows.
Having made this announcement, one should then respond: "So be it."
Regarding the method for formal repentance: the one who repents first confesses all concealed offenses and the like; the method of confession is as follows.
Thereafter, the root offense is removed. To remove the root, one should say:
"Sister, please attend to me with a single mind!"
I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed a certain sthūlātyaya offense. I now confess it before the Venerable Sisters; I dare not conceal it.
Through confession there is peace and happiness; without confession there is no peace and happiness. I recall the offense and disclose it; knowing it, I do not conceal it.
"May the Elder sister remember my purity; my body of precepts is complete, and my uposatha has been performed purely.
This is repeated three times.
The presiding master of the confession says:
Reproach your own mind and give rise to weary detachment.
The one who confesses replies: "So be it."
The method for confessing before three bhikṣuṇīs: regarding the aforementioned offense of a medium-grade sthūlātyaya, one should confess before a small assembly.
That bhikṣuṇī should go to three pure bhikṣuṇīs and request one of them to serve as the presiding master of confession.
The request for the Dharma is as described above.

Once the presiding master of the repentance ceremony has accepted the invitation, he must not grant permission immediately; rather, he shall change the formal announcement (*jñapti*) into an inquiry to those present. He should ask the two bhikṣuṇīs:
"If you two sisters will permit me to receive the confession of the bhikṣuṇī [Name], I shall accept it."
Those two bhikṣuṇīs should reply: "So be it.
Once the presiding master of the confession has obtained the consent of the two bhikṣuṇīs, he then says to the one confessing:
It may be so. The method of repentance is as described above;
however, for a small assembly repentance, three persons are required.

The method for confessing before two persons is identical to this with no difference; however, regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture), it may be performed before two persons.
The method for confessing before one bhikṣuṇī applies to the aforementioned minor *sthūlātyaya* offense; one shall confess before one bhikṣuṇī.

That bhikṣuṇī goes to another pure bhikṣuṇī and requests her to serve as the presiding master for the confession and to perform the formal rite of confession; everything is done exactly as before, with the exception of questioning the bystander.
Regarding the rules for expiating *pāyattika* offenses, these rules consist of two categories:
first, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattikas*; second, the one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattikas*.
Regarding the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, at the time of relinquishing [the object], two types of precious things are excluded.
Whether it be a Saṃgha, a group of many people, or a single individual, one must not relinquish it outside of the assembly (*pṛthag-jana*).
If one relinquishes it in such a manner, the relinquishment is not valid, and it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) for wealth surrendered to the Saṃgha, one must not fail to relinquish the forfeited robe;

rather, one should either make it a *pariśuddha-dāna* (pure gift), give it away to another, make it into the three robes (*tricīvara*), make it into a *pārihārika-cīvara*, intentionally damage it, burn it, use it for something other than a robe, or wear it repeatedly.
That bhikṣuṇī should go before the Saṃgha, assume the proper deportment, and make this formal relinquishment, saying:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have intentionally kept [number] many extra robes—specifying each according to its kind—with the matter being stated individually; having exceeded ten days, I have committed an offense of relinquishment and forfeiture."
"I now relinquish this to the Saṃgha.
(Recite this once.
Regarding the method for relinquishing the offense and requesting confession: after he has finished relinquishing the object, he requests confession from the Saṃgha, making the request as follows.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have intentionally kept an extra robe—specifying its type according to its name—for more than ten days, thereby committing an offense of relinquishment and forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
This robe has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha; herein lie several, numerous *pāyattika* offenses, which I now beg the Saṃgha to accept for confession.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], permission to confess.
Recite this three times.
These ritual procedures for the Sangha are largely the same as those in the preceding section.
Because these *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses are frequently committed by people, yet the formal performance of the rite is difficult, they are described here in further detail.

Regarding the request for a presiding master of confession (*kṣamāpanā-adhipati*): one who wishes to perform confession should request a pure *bhikṣuṇī* from within the Saṃgha to serve as the presiding master of confession.
One should then go to that pure *bhikṣuṇī* and, having prepared the proper ritual deportment, make this request:
"Sister, please attend to me with a single mind!"

I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have intentionally kept [a certain number] of many extra robes—specifying each according to its type and name—for more than ten days; I have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This robe has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha; herein there are several, numerous *pāyattika* offenses, as well as other remaining offenses, which shall likewise be named accordingly.
I now request the Venerable Sister to act as the presiding master for my confession.
"I pray that you, Great Sister, will act as my master of confession out of compassion.
(Recite this once.
The procedure for the master of confession to inform the Saṃgha: The master of confession must not grant permission immediately; rather, they should inform the Saṃgha, saying:
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

The bhikṣuṇī [Name] intentionally kept [a number of] many extra robes—specifying them according to their respective types—and having exceeded ten days, she has committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

This robe has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha; herein there are [certain] numerous *pāyattika* offenses and other remaining offenses as they are named, which I now beg the Saṃgha to accept for my confession.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits me, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
Having made this formal announcement (*jñapti*) in this manner, one should then reply:
It may be so. Regarding the method of formal repentance, the various offenses herein are distinguished by their initial and final stages, totaling twelve positions and three types of offenses.
The first set of three is as follows:
This refers to the long-term *pāyattika* offense, as well as the two types of concealment: the fundamental and the successive.
Regarding the second triad:
when the Saṃgha recites the precepts, one declares oneself pure; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense along with the two types of concealment.
The third set of three:
confessing purity before another during the recitation of the precepts, a *pāyattika* offense, and two instances of concealment.
The fourth set of three:
When the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*, if one declares oneself pure (*śuddhi-ārocana*), there is a *pāyattika* offense and two instances of concealment.
Regarding the fifth triad:
when performing the *pravāraṇā* face-to-face (*pratyekamukha*), if one declares oneself pure, there is a *pāyattika* offense and two instances of concealment.
The third set of the sixth [offenses] consists of:
preaching the precepts to the assembly while one has committed an offense oneself; a *duṣkṛta* offense; and the two types of concealment (*paryuṣita*).
The third set of the seventh [offenses] consists of:
The eighth triad consists of: first, the *duṣkṛta* offense of not being fit to hear the precepts when one has committed an infraction, along with the two concealments;
and second, the *duṣkṛta* offense of lying through silence during the three inquiries made by the Saṃgha when reciting the precepts at two locations, along with the two concealments.
The third of the ninth [category] consists of:
the offense of *duṣkṛta* for mentally intending to recite the *Poṣadha* while claiming one's own purity, and the concealment of the opposite two [offenses].
The third of the tenth [category] consists of: [the same].
The offense of *duṣkṛta* for performing the *pravāraṇā* by mental intimation while claiming one's own purity, along with the two concealments; the eleventh triad is:
having committed an offense oneself and accepting another’s confession of it, [resulting in] the offense of *duṣkṛta* and the two concealments.
The twelfth set of three consists of:
