wearing a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* robe, which constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense along with two periods of concealment (*paṭicchanna*).

Regarding these twelve positions and their three offenses, when performing the confession, one must ascertain whether the conditions for each are complete or deficient, according to the correct interpretation of the texts.
The confession is divided into three stages:

First, the collective confession of the twenty-four concealed offenses (*pācittiya*). This refers to the original *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture) up to the twelfth, as well as the two *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoings) regarding concealment and subsequent concealment when using a discarded robe; these are grouped together because their categories of offense are identical.
Second, one should likewise repent for the seven types of *duṣkṛta* offenses, such as reciting the *Prātimokṣa* together with others, because these seven categories are similar.
Third, one should likewise repent for the five types of *pāyattika* offenses, such as [keeping] an extra robe.

Regarding the method for repenting the twenty-four offenses of concealment: when performing this rite of repentance, one must observe the proper ritual protocol with utmost sincerity and earnestness, maintaining profound gravity and a sense of shame, severing the continuity of the offense forever, and requesting witness and testimony;
if one acts with superficiality or levity, the offense will certainly not be extinguished.
One should act as follows:

"I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], intentionally kept this many long robes—[specifying them according to their respective types]—for more than ten days; I have thus committed this many instances of the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Having committed these offenses, when the Saṃgha recites the Prātimokṣa, he declares himself pure; yet he has committed so many numerous *pāyattika* offenses.
When reciting the Prātimokṣa face-to-face, he declares himself pure; yet he has committed so many numerous *pāyattika* offenses.
When the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*, one declares oneself pure, yet has committed so many numerous *pāyattika* offenses.
When performing the *pravāraṇā* face-to-face with another, one declares oneself pure, yet has committed so many numerous *pāyattika* offenses.
To preach the precepts to the assembly while being guilty of an offense oneself constitutes numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses of such a magnitude.
To listen to the recitation of the precepts while being guilty of an offense oneself is improper; this constitutes numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses of such a magnitude.
When the Saṃgha recites the precepts, if one commits such-and-such numerous offenses through silence during the three formal inquiries, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one commits such-and-such numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses while mentally reciting the precepts and declaring oneself pure.
One commits numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses by performing the *pravāraṇā* through mental reflection while claiming one's own purity;
one commits numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses by accepting the confession of another while being guilty of such and so many offenses oneself.
Regarding the wearing of an *niḥsargika-pāyattika* robe, one commits that many numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses.

Since one recognizes all such offenses but does not disclose them, one commits a *pāyattika* offense of concealment (*sthirana*) after a night has passed; for those who do not remember the number, it is said that they "know the number."

Having already passed the second night, I have again committed the *duṣkṛta* offense of concealing [the transgression] as it was transmitted from one to another; I do not remember the number of times, yet knowing the number, I said I knew.
I now repent and dare not conceal it further.
To repent brings peace and joy; not to repent brings no peace or joy. I now call to mind my transgressions and disclose them; knowing them, I do not conceal them.
I now reproach myself with a sincere heart and give rise to weary detachment.
One interpretation states:
although it is said that the responsibility lies with the mind, the verbal confession must be fully articulated.

When performing the repentance for the seven types of *dukkaṭa* offenses—such as those concerning the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*—one should employ the complete ritual and express sincere remorse, requesting witness as previously described.
One should act as follows:

"I, the bhikṣuṇī [name], intentionally kept this many extra robes—specifying them according to their respective types—for more than ten days; thus I have committed this many instances of the offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
Having committed this offense, he preached the precepts to the assembly; thus he committed numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses for that many instances.
Since he himself possessed an offense, it was improper for him to hear the precepts; thus he committed numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses for that many instances.

When the Saṃgha recites the precepts, if one commits such-and-such numerous offenses through silence when questioned three times at two points, it constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta* for false silence.
If one performs the mental recitation of the precepts and declares oneself pure while having committed such-and-such numerous offenses, it constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
By performing the *pravāraṇā* through mental reflection while claiming one's own purity, one commits numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses of such a magnitude.
By accepting the confession of another while being guilty of an offense oneself, one commits numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses of such a magnitude.
Regarding the wearing of an *niḥsargika-pāyattika* robe, one commits as many or numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses as applicable.
My confession now is the same as before.
The sincere confession for the five categories of *pāyattika* offenses, such as those concerning extra robes, should be performed in this manner.
Sister, attend to me with one-pointed mind!

I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have intentionally kept this many long robes—[specify the type according to the category]—for more than ten days; I have committed an offense of forfeiture and confession (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
This robe has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha; herein lie such a multitude of *pāyattika* offenses.
Having committed these offenses, when the Saṃgha recites the precepts, one declares oneself pure regarding them; yet one has committed such a multitude of *pāyattika* offenses.
When declaring purity through face-to-face recitation of the precepts, one has committed this many numerous *pāyattika* offenses.
When declaring purity during the Sangha’s invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), one has committed this many numerous *pāyattika* offenses.
I confess my purity through the *prātimokṣa* ceremony before the assembly; I have committed this many numerous *pāyattika* offenses.
I now repent before the Venerable Sisters and dare not conceal them.
To confess brings peace and happiness; not to confess brings no peace or happiness. I call to mind my transgression and disclose it; knowing it, I do not conceal it.
May the Elder Sisters remember me as pure, with the body of precepts complete, for the pure *poṣadha*.
After this has been said three times, the one who receives the confession should say:
"Reproach your own mind; you should give rise to weary detachment."
The one performing the confession replies: "Yes.

If the article subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) has already been used up or destroyed, although there is no material object to relinquish, the status of the offense remains the same as before; furthermore, one must know the specific conditions for each instance—whether they were complete or lacking—and perform the confession as described above.

The Method for Returning Garments and Transferring Them on the Spot: If the community of monks is difficult to assemble, or if this bhikṣuṇī has business that requires her to travel far away, she should ask: "To whom shall you give these robes?"
"Give it as she says. It should be done in this manner:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

I, [Name] Bhikṣuṇī, intentionally kept this many long robes—[specify the type as appropriate]—beyond ten days; I have committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) and now forfeit them to the Saṃgha.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall take this robe and give it to that bhikṣuṇī named so-and-so, who shall then return it to this bhikṣuṇī named so-and-so.
The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!

This bhikṣuṇī [Name], intentionally kept such a number of extra robes—[specify the type and quantity]—beyond ten days, thereby committing an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. She now relinquishes them to the Sangha."
The Saṃgha shall take this robe and give it to that bhikṣuṇī so-and-so; that bhikṣuṇī so-and-so shall then return it to this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
Those of you, venerable sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha taking this robe and giving it to that bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, for her to then return it to this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, remain silent.
Whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Sangha has already approved and completed the granting of the robe to that bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so.
Since the Sangha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The rules for the one-month robe, the robe from urgent alms, the storage of robes beyond the permitted period, the bowl, medicine, and the sixteen items are all identical; they differ only in that the specific object is named.

Regarding the method of returning an item after it has been kept overnight: unless there is a superior reason, once the overnight period has passed, a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) must be performed to return it to its owner.
The same applies to the one-month robe and other such items.
Aside from these, one should return the value immediately while seated.
The two methods of returning are identical; it should be done in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

This bhikṣuṇī [Name] intentionally kept this many long robes—[specify the type according to the specific case]—in excess for more than ten days, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture and expiation (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). These robes have now been forfeited to the Sangha.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha take this robe and return it to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

The bhikṣuṇī so-and-so intentionally kept this many long robes—[specify the type as appropriate]—in excess for more than ten days, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). These robes have now been forfeited to the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha returns these robes to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
"Whichever sisters among you approve of the Sangha returning this robe to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak.
The Sangha has approved and finished returning the robe to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so."
Since the Saṃgha has remained silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the rule on not returning an object: once it has been relinquished among the Saṃgha, if one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If one makes it a pure gift (śuddhaka-dāna), or gives it to another person, or takes it to make the three robes (tricīvara), or makes it into a miscellaneous robe (pārikkāra-cīvara), or intentionally damages it, or burns it, or makes it into something that is not a robe, or wears it repeatedly, in all these cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the three *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules for bhikṣuṇīs, one should go before three bhikṣuṇīs, perform the formal ritual, and relinquish [the object] by saying:
"Sisters, please bear this in mind!"
"I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have intentionally kept [an item] and so forth.
The remaining wording is the same as above, with the sole exception that one must not address the Saṃgha.
From among them, one pure Bhikṣuṇī should be requested to serve as the presiding master for the confession; the words of request are as before.

Once the presiding master of the confession has accepted the invitation, he must not grant permission immediately. He should instead modify the formal announcement (*jñapti*) into an inquiry to those nearby, asking the two bhikṣuṇīs:
"If you two, noble sisters, permit me to accept the confession of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, I shall accept it."
Those two bhikṣuṇīs should reply, "So be it.
Once the presiding master of the confession has granted permission, he may then respond to the one confessing:
It is so. The words for the formal confession are the same as those for returning the robe mentioned above;
the inquiry regarding harmony is the same as when one does not return it.
The determination of the offense is the same as above.
If one confesses before two nuns or one nun, each case is identical to this; there is no difference.
In the case of confessing before a single nun, the questioning of a bystander is omitted.
Regarding the method for relinquishing the begging bowl: this relinquishment must be performed before the Saṃgha, and furthermore, it must be at this specific residence and not at another.
Both the words for relinquishing and those for repentance are identical to those previously stated.
The Procedure for Returning the Alms Bowl: If this bhikṣuṇī’s bowl is of high value or of fine quality, it should be set aside; one should take the lowest-quality, inferior bowl and give it to her.
This should be given by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) as follows.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has a bowl that is broken with fewer than five mends and is not leaking, yet she has sought a new bowl; she has thus committed an offense of forfeiture and expiation (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) and now forfeits it to the Sangha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now give this alms-bowl to this bhikṣuṇī [Name].
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has a bowl that is broken with fewer than five mends and is not leaking; yet she has sought a new bowl, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). She now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha;
may the Saṃgha now grant this bowl to this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
"Whichever sisters among you approve of the Sangha giving this bowl to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, remain silent; whichever do not approve, speak.
The Sangha has already approved and completed the granting of this bowl to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so."
The Saṃgha having consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the formal procedure for the distribution of alms-bowls, that bhikṣuṇī’s bowl should be formally announced to the Saṃgha.
The announcement is made as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, let us inquire about this bowl with the Elder in order.
This is the formal motion."
Having made this announcement, one should offer it to the senior monk;
if the senior monk does not accept it, one should give it to that bhikṣuṇī, and she should accept it.
One should not refrain from accepting [an alms bowl] out of a desire to protect the Sangha;
nor should one, for that reason, accept a most inferior bowl. If one accepts such a bowl, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the Elder accepts one, he should give it to the Elder; having taken the Elder’s bowl, he should present it to the next seat.
If the next seat in order takes it, it is exactly as with the senior monk (*sthavira*).
In this manner, it is passed on successively until it reaches the junior-most seat.
Regarding the rule for entrusting the bowl to be held: if one holds this nun’s bowl, one must return it to that nun; or, if one holds the bowl of the junior-most seat, one must give it to her.
When it is time, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) and grant it in this manner:
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

If the Saṃgha deems the time has come and the Saṃgha is willing to grant permission, let the Saṃgha now give this very lowest-ranking bowl—if it is the bowl of this bhikṣuṇī, one should say: 'The Saṃgha now gives this bhikṣuṇī’s lowest bowl'—to [Name] Bhikṣuṇī to keep, until it breaks."
It is announced as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now bestows this—either the bowl of the most junior seat or that bhikṣuṇī’s inferior bowl—to [Name] bhikṣuṇī for her possession, until it breaks."
"Whichever sisters approve of the Saṃgha giving the bowl to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak up.
The Saṃgha has already approved and completed the granting of the bowl to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so."
The Saṃgha having consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

That bhikṣuṇī must protect this bowl: she must not place it where tiles or stones might fall upon it; she must not place it beneath a leaning staff or beneath a leaning sword; she must not place it beneath hanging objects, nor in the middle of a path, nor on top of stones, nor beneath fruit trees, nor on uneven ground. She must not hold two bowls with one hand unless she separates them by her fingers in the center; she must not hold two bowls with one hand while opening a door unless she is being careful. She must not place it inside the threshold or beneath the door leaf; she must not place it beneath a rope bed, a wooden bed, between beds, or at the corner of a bed, except for temporary placement. She must not stand and shake the bowl, even to the point of making it break with her feet; she should not intentionally damage it, intentionally cause it to be lost, or put it to uses other than those for which a bowl is intended.

Regarding the rule for renouncing precious objects among the laity: if a bhikṣuṇī takes gold, silver, or coins with her own hand, or instructs another to take them, or accepts them when they are placed on the ground, she should instruct a trustworthy monastery attendant or an upāsaka, saying:
"This object is not appropriate for me; you should know this."
The method for performing confession before a single person is the same as above.

Regarding the procedure for returning property to a layperson: if that person takes [the items] and returns them to the bhikṣuṇī, she should accept them as belonging to that person and instruct a *kappiya-kāraka* (a steward) to appraise them;
if she obtains pure robes, alms bowls, needle cases, or sitting mats, she should exchange them for items suitable for formal possession.
If a lay follower (upāsaka), having taken [an item], gives it to a bhikṣuṇī as a pure robe, alms bowl, sitting mat (niṣīdana), or needle case, she should accept and keep it.
Regarding the rule that a layperson does not return property: if he takes it and does not return it, one should have another nun say to him:
"You ought to return this object belonging to the bhikṣuṇī."
If other bhikṣuṇīs do not speak [to her], or if they speak but she does not return the answer, she should say to them herself:
"The Buddha taught that bhikṣuṇīs perform the purification (śuddhi) and therefore give it to you. If they say:
One may give it to the Saṃgha, to a stūpa, to one’s preceptor (upādhyāya), and so forth, or to various kinsmen, acquaintances, and friends; or one may return it to its original owner.
Why is this? It is because one does not wish to cause the loss of that faithful offering.
Regarding the purification of jewels, this clarifies the ritual procedure for purifying jewels.
If one follows this section, one may separately designate a faithful upāsaka or a garden keeper as the custodian of the jewels; the jewels should be entrusted to that person, and he should be told:
"This object is not permitted for me; you should take note of this."
Some say: "Know this; look at this.
Or, when receiving [offerings] for the sake of the Buddha-dharma and other such matters, one should use pure speech (*pariśuddha-vāk*) at the time of receiving.
Pure speech should state:
"I know this; I see this.
If one does not speak these words to that person:
To "know this" or "look at this" constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.

According to the *Sarvāstivāda* method for pure giving (*śuddhika-dāna*), regarding money and all precious objects, one should first seek out a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) who understands the Dharma. Having instructed them so that they understand the intent, one should further say:
"It is the rule for us bhikṣuṇīs not to keep money or treasures; I now appoint you, donor, as the pure owner (*śuddhi-svāmī*)."
Afterwards, when money or treasures are obtained, they should all be bestowed upon the donor.
If the steward dies or departs for another country, one should seek a new steward.
Furthermore, there are two ways of declaring things as pure (śuddhi):
If a layperson brings money or precious objects to a bhikṣuṇī and says only:
"This is an impure thing; I should not possess it; if it were pure, I would accept it."
This is a pure dharma.
If a layperson says,
"Give this jewel to a bhikṣuṇī," [the bhikṣuṇī may accept it].
The bhikṣuṇī said: "I should not keep this.
The attendant replied:
To exchange an impure object for a pure one constitutes "purification by exchange" (*parivartana-pariśuddhi*).

If a layperson does not speak of exchanging it for a pure object, and a bhikṣuṇī herself does not perform the declaration of purity (*pāriśuddhi-vyāhāra*), but simply leaves the item on the ground— if there is another bhikṣuṇī present— she should perform the declaration of purity toward her regarding that item, regardless of how long or short the period of possession may be.
The phrasing is the same as above.

Regarding the method for repenting the one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* offenses: if one wishes to eliminate the original offense, one must first repent for the concealment (*tirokaraṇa*). The number of items involved should be understood according to the previous rules.
In this case, confession before a single person is permitted as an alternative to a formal assembly;
one should invite the presiding master of confession and perform the ritual procedures as described above.
Having invited him, one should address the presiding master with these words of confession:
Sister, attend to me with a single mind!

I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have intentionally spoken falsehoods, committing this many pāyattika offenses—[specify the various types according to their names] and [enumerate them individually according to the specific instances].
"I now confess to the elder sister, not daring to conceal it," and so forth,
as above. The method for confessing a *pāyattika* offense regarding the section on concealment is as previously described.
Having requested the presiding master of the confession (*pratideśanā-ācārya*), perform the confession as follows:
"Sister, attend to me with one-pointed mind!

I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], being without illness, intentionally begged for ghee to eat; I have committed such-and-such numerous *pātideśanīya* offenses, [naming them] according to their respective categories and designations."
"Sister! I have committed a blameworthy offense, which ought not to have been done.
I now repent before you, Sister, and dare not conceal it."
The same as above.
One explanation states:

Regarding the method for repenting *duṣkṛta* offenses, all *duṣkṛtas*—whether fundamental or derivative, committed intentionally or through negligence, concealed or followed by concealment—are categorized according to the same number of classes as previously described.
Vowing to sever [these faults] forever, I perform this confession:
I, Bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, intentionally failed to wear the saṃghāṭī in a neat and orderly manner, thereby committing such-and-such numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Because it was done intentionally, he further commits that many numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses of improper conduct (*anācāra*).
If, however, it were committed through negligence, there would be no offense of improper conduct committed intentionally.
One should say:

"I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have mistakenly worn the saṃghāṭī robe in an unneatly manner, thereby committing this many numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses; [the remaining offenses] shall be designated according to their respective names and specific instances."
"I now repent, not daring to conceal [the offense]," and so forth,
as above. Regarding the procedure for all monks to collectively confess recognized offenses, according to the Vinaya:
The Saṃgha gathered in one place intending to recite the precepts. At the time of the recitation, the entire assembly of monks had all committed offenses.
Each of them thought to themselves:

"The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense may not recite the precepts, nor hear the precepts; one may not confess to another who has committed an offense, nor may one who has committed an offense receive the confession of another."
After that bhikṣuṇī has made this announcement, she shall perform confession.
She should make the announcement as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!
This entire assembly of monks has committed an offense.
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha permits it, let this entire Sangha perform confession.
Thus is the motion.
Having made this announcement, the precepts are then recited.
Regarding the rule for the entire Saṃgha to confess a suspected offense when they have collectively committed it, according to the Vinaya:
When the Saṃgha has assembled in one place intending to recite the precepts, at the time of the recitation, the entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding an offense.
Each of them should think to themselves:
"The World-Honored One has established the precepts as before.
After the entire Saṃgha has performed the formal announcement (jñapti), they should confess their offenses.
One should make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding its offenses."
If the time for the Saṃgha has arrived, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: these members of the Saṃgha shall themselves confess their offenses.
This is the formal announcement (jñapti). Having made this announcement, one should then recite the Prātimokṣa.
The method for another person to acknowledge and disclose their offense: One should go to a pure bhikṣuṇī, assume the proper demeanor, and speak as follows:
"Sister, please take note!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense, whether it be a single instance or many."
I now disclose this before the Elder Sister; hereafter, I shall perform repentance according to the Dharma.
(Recited once.
Having done so, one is permitted to hear the precepts.
The method for disclosing another's doubtful offense: Return to a pure bhikṣuṇī and, having performed the proper ritual gestures, speak as follows:
"Sister, please take note!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have developed a doubt regarding a certain offense."
I have now spoken to you, sisters, for yourselves. When you have no further doubts, you should perform the confession according to the Dharma.
This has been said once.
Having done so, you may hear the precepts.
Regarding the procedure for confessing a recognized offense through mental recollection during the *poṣadha* assembly, according to the Vinaya:

if one commits an offense while the *poṣadha* is being recited—whether someone has accused them or not, and whether they have been reminded of it or not—if that person personally recalls the offense and wishes to disclose it, they should say to a neighbor:
"I have committed such-and-such an offense; I now repent before you, Venerable Sister."
She further thinks to herself:
"If I speak to those nearby, I fear it will disturb the assembly and prevent the recitation of the precepts.
That bhikṣuṇī should then form this thought in her mind:
"I have committed such-and-such an offense; I must leave the seat and perform repentance according to the Dharma.
Having done so, I shall be permitted to hear the recitation of the precepts.

The conditions for the method of mentally disclosing a doubtful offense while seated during the recitation of the precepts are the same as those previously described, with the sole difference being that it concerns a doubtful offense.
That person thinks to themselves:
"I have developed doubt regarding a certain offense; once I have risen from my seat and am free from doubt, I shall perform confession according to the Dharma.
Having done this, they may listen to the recitation of the precepts.

Chapter Thirteen: Governing People (Middle). Chapter Thirteen on Governing People, concerning the *karmavācanā* of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*). According to the Vinaya, there are two types of matters for which the Saṃgha should perform the *karmavācanā* of censure:
declaring what is not Dharma to be Dharma, and declaring what is Dharma to be non-Dharma; this applies likewise to cases of speaking and not speaking.
This also applies likewise to the *karmavācanā* of formal accusation (*utksepaṇīya-karman*).
Furthermore, there are three matters for which the Saṃgha should perform the *karma* of censure:
namely, violation of the precepts, violation of views, and violation of dignified conduct;
this applies likewise even to the *karma* of formal accusation.
Furthermore, they delight in quarreling and mutually revile one another, with their mouths spewing swords and blades as they seek out each other's faults;

if others are quarreling, they go there to encourage and assist them. Consequently, they cause disputes to arise where none existed before, and once disputes have arisen, they fail to extinguish them.
Listen as the Saṃgha grants him a formal act of censure through a *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations).
Having assembled the Saṃgha;
once the Saṃgha has assembled, perform the formal act of suspension (*ukṣepa*) against him.
Having performed the formal act of censure, one should provide a reminder;
having provided the reminder, one should impose the offense;
having imposed the offense, one should proceed as follows.
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, delights in quarreling and contending together, reviling one another, and uttering words like swords and blades, seeking out each other's faults.
Having already engaged in mutual quarreling and strife themselves, if there are other bhikṣuṇīs who are quarreling, they immediately go to them and urge them, saying:
"Exert yourselves! Do not be inferior to others!"
"You possess great learning and wisdom, your wealth is superior, and you have many acquaintances;
we shall act as your allies.
Thus they cause disputes to arise where none existed before, and they fail to resolve those that already exist.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so; if she should again engage in quarreling or mutual abuse hereafter, the community of monks shall further increase her punishment.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so delights in quarreling and disputing, reviling one another, uttering words like swords and blades, and seeking out each other's faults."
Having already engaged in mutual strife and contention themselves, if there are other bhikṣuṇīs who are also contending, they immediately go to encourage them, saying:
"Exert yourselves; do not be inferior to others!"
"You possess great wisdom and extensive learning, your wealth is superior, and you have many friends;
we shall act as your allies.
Thus they cause disputes to arise where none existed before in the Sangha, and they fail to resolve disputes that already exist.
The Sangha is performing a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.

Which of you venerable sisters approves of the Sangha’s performance of the *tarjanīya-karman* against the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so? Should she again engage in quarreling or mutual abuse hereafter, the Sangha shall further increase her punishment.
The monks who approve remain silent; those who do not approve should speak.
This has been said three times.
The Sangha has approved and completed the *karman* of censure for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
The Saṃgha having consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Having received the Dharma, he practiced the seven groups of five ascetic observances (*dhūta*).
These seven groups of five are fully explained as above.

The Procedure for the Act of Censure (*tarjanīya-karman*): If the Saṃgha is gathered for the morning meal, the afternoon meal, for preaching the Dharma, or for the Uposatha, the person subject to the act of censure shall adjust their robes, remove their leather sandals, stand to one side, kneel with palms joined, and address them as follows:
"Sisters!"
Accept my confession.
From this day forward, I shall reproach myself and cease, never to do it again.
As the Vinaya says:

If one complies with the Saṃgha and does not oppose it, seeking the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), the lifting shall be granted through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations).
The Saṃgha should examine whether there are five conditions for which the act should not be lifted, namely: if the person violates the aforementioned seven sets of five practices.
There are five things that should be done when granting a resolution for a formal reprimand (*tarjanīya-karman*); that is, one must not violate the aforementioned seven sets of five practices.
One should go before the Saṃgha, assume the proper decorum, and make this request as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!..."
I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have been granted the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) by the Saṃgha.
Now, being in harmony with the Saṃgha and without any opposition, I beg the Saṃgha for the lifting of this *tarjanīya-karman*.
"May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman*.
[Recite] three times.
The Saṃgha should grant the procedure in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has had the *tarjanīyakarman* (act of censure) performed against her by the Saṃgha.
That bhikṣuṇī has complied with the Saṃgha and has not opposed it; she now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *tarjanīyakarman*.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to revoke the *karma* of censure against the bhikṣuṇī [Name].
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the karma of censure.
That bhikṣuṇī has complied with the Saṃgha without opposition and now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the karma of censure.
"Whichever sisters approve of the Sangha's lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman* for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak.
This is said a third time."
The Sangha has already consented to the completion of the *karma* of censure against the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
Because the Sangha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the legal procedure for the *karma* of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), the Vinaya states:
They engage in evil conduct and defile other families.
Regarding "evil conduct," this refers to such acts as planting flower trees oneself or instructing others to do so.
Regarding "defiling a family," there are four types of matters:

First, defiling families by relying on households; second, defiling families by relying on material gain; third, defiling families by relying on relatives and friends; fourth, defiling families by relying on monasteries.

If one has committed evil conduct, defiled the families of others, and is fully established in both what has been seen and heard, the Sangha should perform the formal motion (jñapti) and the fourth proclamation (karma) for his temporary exclusion (pravāsanīya).
The procedures for performing this action and for its subsequent resolution are as clarified in the Vinaya.

Regarding the ritual procedure for granting dependence (*niśraya-karman*): If there is a bhikṣuṇī who is foolish and ignorant, who frequently commits many offenses, who dwells in close association with laypeople, and who does not accord with the Buddha-dharma.
The formal motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) for the Saṃgha to act as one's *niśraya* (spiritual mentor) is as follows:
one is sent to live under the guidance of a virtuous person; however, one must not designate this by referring to a specific region or country.
The procedure for both establishing and releasing this status is also set forth in the Vinaya texts.

The ritual procedure for performing the *karmavācanā* of prohibiting [a monk] from entering the homes of laypeople (*avadhyāna-karma*) is as follows: If a layperson possesses five qualities, the Sangha should perform the *karmavācanā* of prohibiting that person from entering their home:
this person reveres his father, mother, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, and firmly maintains and does not abandon what ought to be upheld.
If a bhikṣuṇī possesses ten qualities, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of *karmavācanā* to prohibit her from entering the homes of laypeople (*avadātavasana*):

she speaks ill of and reviles laypeople; she employs means to cause the decline and loss of lay households; she acts to their disadvantage; she acts to deprive them of a place of residence; she incites strife and discord among laypeople; she slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha in the presence of laypeople; she utters insults regarding lowly and base matters before laypeople; and she promises what is lawful to laypeople but does not fulfill it.
The procedures for performing these acts, as well as assigning duties, sending forth [the offender], and the rites of confession and release, are fully detailed in the Vinaya texts.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* procedure for accusing one who does not acknowledge their offense: if a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense, another bhikṣuṇī says to her, "Do you see that you have committed an offense?"
He replied, “I did not see it.
The Buddha said:
"Listen, the Saṃgha shall perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the purpose of censuring her for not acknowledging her offense.
The procedure for this performance and its subsequent resolution is also as set forth in the Vinaya.
Regarding the ritual for the formal act of censuring one who does not repent their offense: if a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense, the other bhikṣuṇīs say to her:
"You have committed an offense;
you must repent. He replied, "I will not repent."
The Buddha said: "I allow the Saṃgha to perform the formal motion of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the suspension of one who refuses to repent.
The procedures for both its enactment and its rescission are to be conducted according to the text of the Vinaya.
The Procedure for the Formal Act of Suspension for Not Abandoning Evil Views: If a bhikṣuṇī gives rise to such an evil view and speaks thus:
"I know that the Dharma taught by the Buddha—that the commission of sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path."
The Buddha said:
"I permit the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to reprimand him, so that he may relinquish this matter.
The method of admonition is as set forth in the text.
After that bhikṣuṇī had been formally admonished by the Saṃgha, she still did not abandon her evil view.
The Buddha said:
"Perform the formal act of suspension for not abandoning an evil view (akuśaladṛṣṭy-asthāpana) by means of a jñapti-caturtha-karman."
The performance and rescission of this [act] are also as set forth in the Vinaya.
Regarding the ritual for the *kṣiptacitta-karman* (the formal act for one who is insane or deluded), there are three types of insanity or delusion:

first, at the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), one either remembers or does not remember [the offense], and either attends or does not attend; second, one remembers and attends; third, one neither remembers nor attends.
These are called the three types of insanity.
Among them, the latter two should not have [legal acts] performed for them;
for the first, one should perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation).
It should be granted in this manner:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṅgha, please listen!
This bhikṣuṇī [Name] is mentally deranged and insane; she may or may not remember the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, and she may or may not attend."

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so for the purpose of dealing with mental derangement and insanity; whether she remembers or does not remember, whether she comes or does not come, the Saṃgha shall perform the formal act and recite the Prātimokṣa.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so is mentally disturbed, deranged, and insane; she may or may not remember the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, and she may or may not come."

The Saṃgha has performed the *cittavikṣepa-unmāda-karman* for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so; whether she remembers or does not remember, whether she comes or does not come, the *karman* and the recitation of the precepts shall be carried out.

Whichever sisters among you consent to the Saṃgha performing the formal act (*kamma*) and reciting the *Prātimokṣa* for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so—who is mentally disturbed, insane, or deluded, whether she remembers or does not remember, or whether she comes or does not come—remain silent; whoever does not consent, please speak.

The Sangha has already consented to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, who is mentally deranged and insane, whether she remembers or not, and whether she comes or not. The formal act is concluded.
Because the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld. Regarding the lifting of the *karma* for those who are insane or deluded:
if the madness ceases, the Saṃgha shall perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) to lift it.
Having performed the formal ritual, she should make this request:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], previously suffered from the affliction of insanity."
During the recitation of the precepts, whether I remembered or forgot, whether I came or did not come, the Saṃgha performed the *kamma* for insanity against me.
Now that the illness has ceased, I beg the Saṃgha to revoke the *kamma* for insanity.
This is said three times.
The Saṃgha should grant the legal procedure in this manner:
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, was previously afflicted with the disease of insanity.

When the *poṣadha* was being recited, she sometimes remembered and sometimes did not remember; sometimes she came and sometimes she did not come. The Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for her regarding the disease of insanity.
Once the *karmavācanā* had been performed for him, his madness and delusion were brought to an end. He now requests the Saṃgha for the lifting of the *karmavācanā* for madness and delusion.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant the lifting of the *karmavācanā* for madness and delusion.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, was previously afflicted with the disease of insanity."
When he was reciting the precepts, whether he remembered them or not, and whether he came or not, the community of monks performed the *karmavācanā* for him regarding his insanity.
Now that his insanity has ceased since the *karmavācanā* was performed, he requests from the community the lifting of the *karmavācanā* for insanity.
"Whichever sisters approve of the Sangha's granting of the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the formal act of insanity for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak up.
The Sangha has approved and completed the granting of the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the formal act of insanity for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so."
The Saṃgha, by remaining silent, consents; thus this matter is upheld.
The Buddha said:
"Administer the *karmavācanā* for him according to the duration of his insanity."
"The madness has ceased; he has returned to his senses.
Regarding the *karmavācanā* ritual for families under restriction: there was once the home of a lay devotee where both husband and wife had attained faith and joy, becoming disciples of the Buddha.
It is the constant law for the disciples who have seen the Truth under the various Buddhas:
they have no attachment or惜惜 (cherishing) toward the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, even unto their own flesh.

If bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs come to their homes, [the householders] always provide them with food, drink, and various offerings; thus, they cause [the householders] to become impoverished, until their clothing and food are completely exhausted.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the Saṃgha to perform the *karmavācanā* for that householder as a 'family under training' (*śaikṣakula*).
It should be performed in this manner.
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
In a certain city, at the home of a certain lay devotee, the husband and wife have gained faith and become disciples of the Buddha, until their wealth and possessions were completely exhausted.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now perform the *karmavācanā* for this family as a "family under training" (*śaikṣakula-karman*), such that no bhikṣuṇīs shall accept food or eat at that household.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!
In such-and-such a city, at the home of such-and-such a lay devotee, the husband and wife have gained faith and become disciples of the Buddha; their wealth has been entirely exhausted."
The Saṃgha now performs the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for such-and-such a person; no bhikṣuṇīs shall accept food to eat from that household.
Those of you, sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha performing the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for such-and-such a layperson, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already consented to perform the *karmavācanā* for the householder so-and-so as a "family under discipline" (*śikṣādattaka*).
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

There is no offense if one has previously accepted an invitation, if one is ill, if the gift is placed on the ground, if it is received from another person, or if, after the family under discipline has given, their wealth subsequently increases again.

The *karmavācanā* for lifting the *śikṣādattaka* (probation) from a family: If the wealth and goods of the family have increased again, they may request from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *śikṣādattaka-karman*. The Saṃgha should lift it by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
It should be performed in this manner.
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

In a certain city, at the home of a certain layperson, a husband and wife have gained faith and become disciples of the Buddha. They were fond of giving until their wealth was exhausted, so the Sangha previously performed the *kula-karma* (formal act) regarding them as a family under restriction.
Now that their wealth has increased again, they request from the Sangha the lifting of the *kula-karma*."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to revoke the *karmavācanā* of the family under restriction.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

In a certain city, at the home of a certain lay devotee, a husband and wife have gained faith and become disciples of the Buddha. They were fond of giving until their wealth was completely exhausted, so the Sangha previously performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of declaring them a family under training) for them.
Now that their wealth has increased again, they request from the Sangha the lifting of the *śikṣādattaka-karman*.
The Saṃgha now grants the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the "householder-restriction" (*śikṣādattaka*) for the lay devotee [Name].

Those of you, Venerable Sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha granting the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the householder-restriction for the lay devotee [Name], remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to the completion of the *karmavācanā* for the revocation of the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for the lay follower [Name].
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the procedure for the *anyavāda-karman*: if a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense and the bhikṣuṇīs ask her:
"Do you know for yourself that you have committed an offense?
She then replied to the bhikṣuṇīs with another matter:
"To whom were you speaking?"
What matter did you speak of?
What principle did you discuss?
Were you speaking to me?
"To whom are you speaking?
Who has committed an offense?
From what does this offense arise?"
"I do not see any fault!
Why do you say that I am at fault?
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is permitted that after the formal announcement (jñapti) has been made, one shall be designated as 'one who speaks otherwise.
The announcement should be made as follows:
'May the venerable Saṃgha listen!'"
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, has committed an offense. The bhikṣuṇīs asked her:
"Do you now recognize that you have committed an offense?"
That bhikṣuṇī then replied to the other bhikṣuṇīs with a different matter, saying:
"To whom did you speak? What matter were you discussing?"
In discussing what principle,
are you speaking for my sake,
or are you speaking for the sake of others?
Who commits the offense?
From what does the offense arise?
I do not perceive an offense!
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the nun named [Name] be designated as one who speaks evasive words.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having made this motion, she is designated as one who speaks evasive words."
If one utters extraneous speech before the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, it is entirely *duṣkṛta*;
if one utters extraneous speech after the announcement has already been made, it is entirely *pāyattika*.

The Procedure for the Act of Causing Disturbance: If there is a bhikṣuṇī who, after the Saṃgha has established a rule that she must not engage in evasive speech, proceeds to disturb the Saṃgha—by not coming when told to come, coming when not told to come, not rising when she ought to rise, rising when she ought not to rise, not speaking when she ought to speak, or speaking when she ought not to speak.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-karman* (a formal motion) for this bhikṣuṇī, termed 'causing vexation.
The motion is made as follows:"
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, having been designated by the Saṃgha as one who speaks evasively, has thereby provoked and disturbed the community:

when told to come she does not come; when told not to come she comes; when she ought to rise she does not rise; when she ought not to rise she rises; when she ought to speak she does not speak; and when she ought not to speak she speaks."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of patience, grant its consent to designate the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as "one who causes provocation.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having made this motion, she is designated by the Saṃgha as "one who causes provocation."
If one disturbs the Saṃgha before the formal announcement (jñapti) has been made, it is entirely a duṣkṛta offense;
if one disturbs the Saṃgha after the formal announcement has already been made, it is entirely a pāyattika offense.
The method for disciplining a wicked horse: Suppose there is a bhikṣuṇī who is of a wicked nature and does not accept admonition, frequently committing many offenses.
Other bhikṣuṇīs say to her:
"Do you see that you have committed an offense?"
He replied, "I did not see it.
The Sangha should then dismiss him without further questioning, speaking as follows:

If you do not now see your offense, wherever you go, they there shall also raise the charge against you, make it their own declaration for you, and neither allow you to perform an *amūḷhavinaya*, nor allow you to participate in the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*.
Just as a horse trainer, when a wicked horse is difficult to tame, discards the tethering rope and stake;
so too it is with you, bhikṣuṇī, who do not perceive your own faults—you shall likewise be entirely cast aside.
"Wherever you go, you shall not even be permitted to participate in the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*.
This person should not seek permission; this itself constitutes permission.

Regarding the method of disciplinary action by the *brahmadanda*: if there is a bhikṣuṇī who is of evil character, violates the precepts, and refuses to accept admonition, she is to be subjected to the disciplinary action of silent exclusion (*tūṣṇīka-pravāsanīya*).
It should be done in this manner:
all bhikṣuṇīs shall silently exclude her and not speak with her; this is the punishment of brahmadanda.

If she still does not reform, they shall bring her before the assembly, and everyone together shall censure and expel her, neither reciting the precepts with her nor engaging in any communal Dharma activities with her.

At a time when the rules for monks were not being observed, the group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika bhikṣus) and śrāmaṇeras came to the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs and stayed together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs. They mocked one another, sometimes chanting together, sometimes wailing together, and sometimes laughing and playing together, thereby disturbing the bhikṣuṇīs who were practicing meditation.
The Buddha permitted that they be summoned and punished.
If they do not reform, one should perform the *akaraṇīya-karman* (the rite of non-prostration) against the preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and instructors (*ācārya*) of those śrāmaṇeras.
The procedures for performing and rescinding this rite are as clarified in the Vinaya.
Regarding the legal procedure for performing the *pātra-nyubja* (turning down the bowl) against a lay family, the Vinaya states:
There are five conditions under which one should not perform the *pātra-nyubja* against a lay family:
being unfilial toward one's father; being unfilial toward one's mother; being disrespectful toward śramaṇas; being disrespectful toward brāhmaṇas; and failing to provide service to bhikṣuṇīs.
There are five things that should not be done; these are the opposites of the aforementioned [five].
Furthermore, there are ten things for which the Saṃgha should perform the *pātra-nyāsa* (suspension of the bowl) against a person:

reviling and slandering a bhikṣuṇī; acting to the detriment of a bhikṣuṇī; acting to her disadvantage; using skillful means to deprive her of a dwelling place; inciting strife among bhikṣuṇīs; speaking ill of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha in the presence of a bhikṣuṇī; slandering a bhikṣuṇī with groundless charges of unchastity; or committing an offense against a bhikṣuṇī.
In this manner, down to nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one, the *pātrāvarṣaṇīya-karman* (the formal act of overturning the bowl) should be performed.
It should be performed as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!..."
This person, [Name], though pure, has been slandered by the bhikṣuṇī [Name] with groundless charges of a pārājika offense.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now perform the act of overturning the alms-bowl for this person, [Name], so that there shall be no mutual association.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This person, [Name], has falsely slandered the nun [Name] with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense, even though she is pure."
Now the Saṃgha shall perform the *pātra-nyubja* (turning-over of the bowl) rite against [Name], such that there shall be no mutual interaction.
Any of you, Venerable Sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha performing the *pātra-nyubja* rite against [Name] so that there shall be no mutual interaction, remain silent; any who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to perform the *pātra-āvartana* (turning over of the bowl) for [Name], prohibiting mutual association, and the matter is concluded.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus.
The legal procedure for appointing a bhikṣuṇī to inform a layperson is as follows:
One should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to appoint a certain bhikṣuṇī as a messenger to inform the other party.
That bhikṣuṇī messenger must possess eight qualities.
These eight qualities and the procedure for her appointment are explained in detail in the Vinaya.
This messenger bhikṣuṇī should go to that household and must not accept offerings such as seats, bedding, food, drink, or other requisites; she should say:
"The Saṃgha has now performed the *pātra-nyubja* (turning-over of the bowl) for you, and we shall no longer have mutual dealings."
If they do not understand, you should explain it to them in detail.
If that person says,
"By what means can my bowl be uncovered so that we may once again come and go [to one another]?"
The messenger should say:
"You ought to go and confess before the Saṃgha.

If he confesses, follows the Saṃgha, does not dare to oppose it, and requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātra-nikubjana* (the overturning of the bowl) so that they may once again interact with one another, the Saṃgha should lift it for him.
The phrasing is as in the Vinaya.
[This concludes] the middle fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-karman* and the lower fascicle of the *Bhikṣuṇī-karman*, extracted from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of Xitaiyuan Temple, Volume 14:
Chapter Fourteen on Offering Counsel (Part Two). Chapter Fourteen on Offering Counsel:

Regarding the Dharma for Counseling a Monk Who Has Been Subjected to Formal Accusation. At that time, the monk Chanda was subjected to a formal accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) by the community of monks in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions; yet he did not comply, did not repent, and the Saṃgha had not yet granted him restoration to communal life.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Ucchā who went back and forth to serve the bhikṣu Channa.
The Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to reprimand the bhikṣuṇī Ucchā."
The bhikṣuṇīs said to this bhikṣuṇī:

"This bhikṣu has been subject to a formal act of suspension by the Saṃgha—done in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha's instructions—and he has neither complied nor repented; therefore, the Saṃgha has not yet granted him communal residence."
Do not comply with this; you should abandon this matter so that you do not become subject to formal censure by the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense.
If you follow these words, it is well; if you do not follow these words, a formal announcement (jñapti) shall be made.
Having made the announcement, one should further say:
"Sister, you should know that I have already made the announcement; there remains the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).
You must relinquish this matter, lest you be formally charged by the Saṃgha and commit a grave offense once again."
If she complies with these words, it is well; if she does not comply, you should perform the first *karmavācanā*.
Having performed the first *karmavācanā*, you should say to her:
"Sister!"
I have already performed for you the first *jñapti-karman*; two *karman*s remain.
You should relinquish this matter; do not be censured by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense.
If she complies with these words, it is well; if she does not comply, a second *karmavācanā* should be performed.
Having performed the second *karmavācanā*, one should speak to her again:
"Sister, do you understand?"
I have already performed the first of the two *jñapti-karman* motions; only one motion remains.
You should abandon this matter, lest you be formally charged by the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense.
If she complies with what is said, it is well; if she does not comply, the third *karmavācanā* (formal act) is performed.
When the third *karmavācanā* is completed, it is a *pārājika*.
If she desists after the second *karmavācanā* has been completed, there are three *sthūlātyaya*s.
If one renounces [the offense] after the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the first *karma* have been completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If one renounces it after the formal motion has been completed, there is one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one renounces it before the formal motion has been completed, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If, before the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one follows and accords with the monk who has been accused, it is an *āpatti* of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in all such cases.
The essential nature of the ritual procedure (*karman*) is fully explained in the Vinaya.

Regarding the method for admonishing one who would split the Saṃgha: if a bhikṣuṇī, through skillful means, desires to split the harmonious Saṃgha, accepts the methods for splitting the Saṃgha, and persists in holding to them without relinquishing them.
That bhikṣuṇī should admonish this bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister! Do not employ means to break the harmonious Saṃgha; do not accept the dharma of breaking the Saṃgha, nor persist in holding to it without relinquishing it."

"Sister! You should be in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing and not disputing, like water and milk blended as one, so that you may find increase, benefit, and dwell in peace within the Buddha-dharma."
"Sister! You should abandon this matter so that the Saṃgha does not issue a formal admonition and you do not incur a grave offense.

It would be well if you were to follow this advice; if you do not follow it, we shall further summon bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as kings, ministers, various heretical śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, or bhikṣuṇīs from other regions who know of this person and whose words are trusted and believed—these should come."
If they accept what you say, it is well; if they do not accept what you say, you should make a formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Having made the announcement, you should further request:
"Sister!..."
I have finished the motion; there remains the formal act (*karmavācanā*).
You should now relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform the formal act against you and cause you to incur a further grave offense.
If she accepts the instruction, it is well; if she does not accept the instruction, one should perform the first *karmavācanā*.
Having performed the first *karmavācanā*, one should further request:
"Sister!..."
I have already completed the first *karmavācanā* proclamation; two more remain.
You should relinquish this matter so that the Saṃgha does not perform the *karmavācanā* for you again, lest you incur a grave offense.
If she accepts what is said, it is well; if she does not accept what is said, one should perform the second *karmavācanā*.
Having performed the second, one should further request her, saying:
"Sister!..."
I have already completed the first of the two formal motions (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*); only one motion remains.
You should relinquish this matter so that the Saṃgha does not perform the formal motion for you again, whereby you would incur a grave offense.
If she is able to relinquish it, that is well; if she is unable to relinquish it, the third *karmavācanā* is recited to her.
Once the third *karmavācanā* has been completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one renounces [the offense] after the second motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) have been completed, there are three *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If one renounces it after the first motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-ekakaraṇa-karman*) have been completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If, after the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been completed, he abandons [the position], it is one *sthūlātyaya*.
If he abandons it before the initial announcement is finished, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If, prior to any announcement whatsoever, he employs the means to split the harmonious Saṃgha, accepts the method for splitting the harmonious Saṃgha, and persists in holding to it without abandoning it, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The essential nature of the *karmavācanā* procedure is fully explained in the Vinaya.

Regarding the method for admonishing those who assist in schism: when the Saṃgha is admonishing a bhikṣuṇī who is causing a schism, there may be other bhikṣuṇīs belonging to an unlawful faction—whether one, two, three, or many—who say to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Sisters!..."
"Do not admonish this bhikṣuṇī; this bhikṣuṇī is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya;
what this bhikṣuṇī has said, we accept."
The bhikṣuṇīs should say to her: "Do not speak these words, saying:
'This bhikṣuṇī is a bhikṣuṇī who speaks according to the Dharma; this bhikṣuṇī is a bhikṣuṇī who speaks according to the Vinaya.'"
"What this bhikṣuṇī has said, we accept and approve.
Yet, this bhikṣuṇī speaks what is not in accordance with the Dharma; she speaks what is not in accordance with the Vinaya.
"You should not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead support the harmony of the Saṃgha. Sisters!
Be in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing together and free from dispute."
As before, the essential nature of the *karmavācanā* ritual is also as clarified in the Vinaya.

Regarding the method for admonishing a nun who has been expelled for slandering the Saṃgha: if there is a bhikṣuṇī who commits evil deeds and defiles families, and this is fully established through both what has been seen and heard.
When the Saṃgha performed the formal act of banishment, she slandered the Saṃgha, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs have favoritism, malice, fear, and delusion; for there are bhikṣuṇīs who have committed such identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not."
The bhikṣuṇīs should say to her: "Sister!
We have both seen and heard that you defile families, and we have both seen and heard that you engage in evil conduct."
"Sister! You have defiled families and committed evil deeds; abandon this matter so that you do not incur the censure of the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense.
It would be well if you follow these words."
If she does not comply with her words, the procedure continues up to the third admonition as described above.
The formal substance of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is also as clarified in the Vinaya.

Regarding the method for admonishing a nun of evil character who does not accept counsel: if there is a bhikṣuṇī of evil character who does not accept the words of others, and the other bhikṣuṇīs instruct her according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, yet she herself acts in such a way that she cannot be spoken to, and says to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Sisters! Do not speak to me of what is good or bad, nor shall I speak to you, sisters, of what is good or bad.
Sisters, stop!"
"There is no need to admonish me.
That bhikṣuṇī then admonished this bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Sister!"
Do not make yourself one with whom it is impossible to converse; rather, you should become one with whom it is possible to converse.
Sister, you should admonish the bhikṣuṇīs in accordance with the Dharma, and the bhikṣuṇīs should likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, the community of the Buddha’s disciples gains increase as they instruct one another, admonish one another, and repent before one another. Sister!
You should abandon this matter; do not be censured by the Sangha and commit a further grave offense.
If they comply with what is said, it is well;
if they do not comply, it shall proceed up to the third time as described above.
The formal substance of the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion and three proclamations) is also as clarified in the Vinaya.

When admonishing regarding the practice of living in close association, there were two bhikṣuṇīs, one named Soma and the other named Vappā, who constantly lived together, committed evil deeds in concert, spread an evil reputation, and repeatedly concealed their offenses from one another.
Other bhikṣuṇīs said to them: "Sisters!
You two should not stay close together, committing evil deeds and spreading an evil reputation, while covering one another's offenses."

If you do not associate with one another, do not commit evil deeds together, do not spread an evil reputation, and instead mutually conceal each other's offenses, then within the Buddha-dharma, there will be increase and you shall dwell in peace and happiness.
Yet he still did not desist. The Buddha said: "I allow the Saṃgha to perform a formal admonition against him;
for the sake of making him abandon this matter, a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) shall be carried out."
Other bhikṣuṇīs admonished those bhikṣuṇīs, saying: "Sisters!
Do not associate with one another, do not engage in evil conduct together, do not spread an evil reputation, and do not conceal each other's offenses."

If you do not associate with one another and engage in unwholesome conduct, so that an evil reputation does not spread, you will attain increase, benefit, peace, and happiness within the Buddha-dharma.
"You should all desist from this matter; do not be censured by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense.
If you comply with these words, it is well;
if you do not comply, the procedure shall be repeated up to the third time, as described above."
The formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is also as clarified in the Vinaya.

When the monks were admonishing the two bhikṣuṇīs who had lived in close association with those who slandered the Saṃgha and encouraged such associations, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs instructed them to say:
"You should continue to live together."

Why is this? I have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs living together, associating with one another, committing evil deeds together, spreading an evil reputation together, and concealing their offenses from one another.
"Because the Saṃgha was moved by anger, they instructed you to dwell separately.
The Buddha said,
"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of censure (*tajjanīya-karma*) consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) against the group of six bhikṣuṇīs."
That bhikṣuṇī should admonish that other bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister! Do not instruct other bhikṣuṇīs, saying:..."
"Do not live separately; you should live together.
I have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs who were closely associated with one another, committed evil deeds together, spread an evil reputation, and covered for each other's offenses."
"Because of their anger, the Saṃgha has instructed you to dwell separately.

Now there are only these two bhikṣuṇīs and no others; yet you have associated with one another, committed evil deeds together, spread an evil reputation, and covered for each other's offenses. If these bhikṣuṇīs were to dwell separately, there would be increase and peaceful dwelling within the Buddha-dharma.
"You should now relinquish this matter; do not be censured by the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense.
If you comply with these words, it is well;
if you do not comply, then proceed as above up to the third time."
The formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is also as clarified in the Vinaya.

Regarding the method of admonishing those who, out of anger, abandon the Triple Gem: at that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, provoked by some trivial matter, became angry and displeased, and spoke these words:

"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha. It is not only this śramaṇa son of the Śākyas that exists; there are other śramaṇas and brahmins who practice the holy life, and we may likewise practice the holy life under them."
The Buddha said:

"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of censure (tarjanīya-karman) by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations), in order that she may relinquish this matter.
Then, that bhikṣuṇī should admonish the other bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister! Do not, out of anger and displeasure over a mere trifle, speak thus:

'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha; there are not only these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, but there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life, and we may also practice the holy life under them.'"
"Abandon this matter; do not incur further grave offenses by being rebuked by the Saṃgha.
If you comply with these words, it is well;
if you do not comply, then up to the third time, as stated above."
The substance of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) is also as clarified in the Vinaya.

At the time when the practice of admonishing those who incite the four types of disputes and slander the Saṃgha was being established, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Kālī who delighted in quarreling and was not skilled at remembering the details of a dispute.
Later, she became resentful and spoke these words: "The Saṃgha has favoritism, anger, fear, and delusion."
The Buddha said:

"I permit the Saṃgha to carry out a formal act of censure against the bhikṣuṇī Kālī by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations), in order that she may relinquish this matter.
That bhikṣuṇī should then admonish the other bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister! Do not take pleasure in quarreling, nor poorly retain the matters of dispute, and later, out of anger, speak these words:
'The Saṃgha has favoritism, has ill will, has fear, and has delusion.'"
"The Saṃgha is without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion; it is you who possess attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion.
You should now abandon this matter, lest you be censured by the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense."
If they comply with what has been said, it is well;
if they do not comply, up to the third time, as stated above. The formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is also as clarified in the Vinaya.
Regarding the admonition against holding wrong views that claim sensual desire does not obstruct the path to enlightenment:
If there is a bhikṣuṇī who speaks thus, saying, "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual desire is not a factor that obstructs the path."
The virtuous bhikṣuṇīs should admonish this bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the Blessed One. It is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One; the Blessed One does not speak such things."
The World-Honored One has, through countless skillful means, taught that engaging in sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path.
You should now abandon this matter, lest you be rebuked by the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense.
If they comply with what has been said, it is well;
if they do not comply, the procedure continues up to the third time as described above.
The formal substance of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is also as clarified in the Vinaya.
The method for admonishing *śikṣamāṇās* and *śrāmaṇerīs* is the same as this, without difference.

Regarding the method for admonishing those who associate with the sons of householders: at one time, there were bhikṣuṇīs who associated with householders and the sons of householders, living together with them and engaging in improper conduct.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs admonished her, saying:
"Do not associate with laymen or the sons of laymen, nor engage in conduct that is unbecoming. You!..."
"Sister!
You should dwell apart.
If you dwell apart, you will attain increase in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma."
Yet she still did not live separately.
The Buddha said:

"I permit the Saṃgha to carry out a formal act of censure against that bhikṣuṇī by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations), in order to make her abandon this matter."
Those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister!
Do not associate with householders or the sons of householders, nor engage in conduct that is unbecoming."
"You should dwell apart; if you dwell apart, there will be increase and peace within the Buddha-dharma.
You should now abandon this matter, lest you be censured by the Saṃgha and commit a grave offense."
If they comply with what has been said, it is well;
if they do not comply, this is repeated up to the third time as above.
The formal substance of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is also as clarified in the Vinaya.

The Rule for Admonishing One Who Commits an Offense: If there is a bhikṣuṇī who intends to commit an offense ranging from a pārājika down to an improper speech (durbhāṣita), the other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī in accordance with the Dharma, saying:
"Sister!..."
"Do not do this; this should not be done. What you have done, Sister, is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to what the Buddha has taught.
Yet this bhikṣuṇī did not heed the lawful exhortations of the virtuous bhikṣuṇīs, and she has thus committed an offense."
If this bhikṣuṇī knows for herself that what she has done is right and that the admonition of others is wrong, yet she persists in doing it, she commits a root offense;
if she does not comply with their words, she commits a duṣkṛta.
If this bhikṣuṇī knows that what she has done is wrong and clearly understands that the admonition of others is right, yet she persists in her action, she commits a root offense;
if she does not comply with their words, it is a pāyattika.
If there is an ignorant person who does not know the method of admonition, one should say to them:
"You should ask your preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya), further study, inquire, and recite the scriptures; once you have learned the method of admonition, you may then offer your counsel."
This method of admonition applies generally to the prevention of transgressions; it differs from the formal admonitions of the Saṃgha, which are established separately according to specific matters.
